<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSat, 10 Oct 2026 18:46:11 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[We have just seen a perfect example of Ireland’s fiscal incontinence]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/10/david-mcwilliams-we-have-just-seen-a-perfect-example-of-irelands-fiscal-incontinence/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/10/david-mcwilliams-we-have-just-seen-a-perfect-example-of-irelands-fiscal-incontinence/Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Nothing focuses the mind like a hanging,” noted Samuel Johnson, according to his biographer James Boswell. The condemned man, realising that he has only a few weeks to live, focuses on what is truly important. The economic equivalent of this expression is: “Nothing focuses the mind like a hard budget.” Hard budgets make countries and organisations efficient, innovative, thoughtful and, by injecting financial discipline, ensure that decision-makers work through their options to get value for money. The hard budget in itself leads to better management, getting more from less, which requires more effort.

In contrast, a sloppy, bloated budget where money is not a problem will lead to waste, cynicism, cutting corners and the abandonment of accounting discipline. When money is wasted, the essential connection between the cost of something and the delivery of quality breaks down.

Without a hard budget, management becomes almost impossible and the corporation, organisation or country drifts, becoming gradually unable to deal with any shocks to the system that might lie ahead. Like someone who allows themselves to get out of shape, their muscles to weaken, and their weight to soar, the person becomes more susceptible to physical and potential emotional or psychological fragility.

Countries and corporations operate in a similar fashion. If they become addicted to easy money, particularly if that money is someone else’s, a gap opens up between reality and fantasy. The managers begin to feel that the money is theirs and they are entitled to it, creating a dependency. Successful management no longer revolves around the best use of the resources to achieve a specific outcome, but rather it becomes a smash-and-grab exercise centred on how much of the “easy” money the managers can get their hands on.

Without a budget constraint, the objective of management becomes size, not efficiency. The organisation becomes an extractive machine, extracting money from the central budget and, as that part of the organisation gets bigger, the fact of its expanding size means that it gobbles up more and more money, needing more every year just to stay still.

This is what has happened to the Irish State. It is a monstrously bloated organisation that has lost all sense of value for money and exists to gorge on cheap, endless cash that is cascading into the coffers from the US multinationals.

In development economics this process, whereby the State becomes hollowed out by too much rather than too little money, is termed the ”resource curse”. When an underdeveloped country without proper institutions finds a resource like oil, money flows in and it is often wasted, ending up in the pockets of the rulers, driving up costs for everyone else. The country ends up unbalanced – rich in parts but without the public infrastructure that the financial windfall could have paid for. Think Nigeria, Angola or Venezuela, where huge oil finds have not elevated the position of the citizens who own the natural resources of the country.

If these countries are synonymous with bad management, the exemplar of good behaviour is Norway, where the oil windfall has been invested judiciously and democratically for future generations, rather than blown on goodies for today.

Now look at Ireland’s equivalent of an oil find – the gusher that is the US multinational money, a spigot of cashflow, the product of clever tax arbitrage, which is flowing into the system to be pilfered by public sector management in a country that can’t even build a proper national rail system.

This week’s budget is a perfect example of the fiscal incontinence that a soft budget generates. First the Government flatters to deceive by announcing an overall surplus of about €9 billion next year. This looks great, but when you consider that the Department of Finance regards about €23 billion of the €34 billion in projected corporation taxes received this year as being transient, then we are in a different world. If we were to strip that out, our underlying surplus becomes a significant deficit of €13 billion to €14 billion for 2027; and, given commitments outlined in this budget, that deficit will widen to about €20 billion by 2029.

Even from a cyclical perspective, a country at full employment does not need any more money thrown at it – the economy is already bursting at the seams – and yet this week’s Budget 2027 is throwing a net €7.4 billion extra into an already bloated system.

New public spending efficiency taskforce to be established within three months

The Government presents it as cost-of-living relief. But the cost of living has risen because prices have risen. Throwing extra money at this problem will not cause prices to fall, but will cause them to rise, while the extra handout to soften the blow will simply increase dependency on handouts rather than cut prices and permanently. So you get the worst of all worlds: handouts which drive prices higher that are mistakenly put forward as a solution to high prices.

The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council’s analysis says spending is growing at double the pace of the Government’s own 5 per cent sustainable limit. Basically, our windfall is being spent rather than saved.

The lack of a hard budget also means that tough decisions are not taken, not just in the area of financial management but in organisational management too. Take, for example, this rotating taoiseach codology. With two bosses – one on the way out, the other on the way in – the lad on the way in is more important for tomorrow, undermining the lad in situ today.

Such management structure means that the incentive for all senior public servants and politicians is to curry favour with the next guy, not the guy in charge, thus undermining the guy in charge.

And by splitting the Department of Finance in two, with the Department of Finance and the Department of Public Expenditure, what’s the aim? Rather than have one department looking after the money, we now have two departments – and, critically, the Department of the Taoiseach, which used to be the nerve centre of final decision making, is now neutered because no one knows which taoiseach is more important: the incumbent or the next guy.

All the while global financial markets, the font of the windfall money that finances the large US tech companies, are becoming more and more nervous about the future.

]]>Clodagh Kilcoyne<![CDATA[Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: How does it work if I have €1 or €12,000 to put in?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/09/irelands-new-personal-investment-accounts-what-you-need-to-know/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/09/irelands-new-personal-investment-accounts-what-you-need-to-know/Fri, 09 Oct 2026 12:23:26 +0000Budget 2027 was, in keeping with the personality of the Minister for Finance Simon Harris, an exercise in soundbites – a little across a wide range of areas for everyone. The one exception was the personal investment account.

First flagged back in February, Harris finally provided some of the key details that will govern how people can use these accounts.

With the Central Statistics Office reporting strong savings by households and more than €170 billion sitting in bank deposits – most earning little or nothing in interest – he hopes the new accounts will encourage people to take a little risk with their money in the hope of better returns while providing funding that can help Irish businesses grow.

It’s a move that harks back to the great (and ultimately disastrous) exercise in widespread public engagement with the stock markets that was the flotation of Telecom Éireann.

The Government will hope fervently for a different outcome this time around. The last thing it needs come the next general election is disgruntled investors in a government-sponsored scheme who have lost some of their money.

What is a personal investment account?

The personal investment account allows individuals above a certain age to put some money into tax efficient investments rather than keeping it in cash on deposit at their local bank or with An Post or a credit union.

How does it work?

Harris said in the budget that people will be allowed to invest up to €12,000 a year in an account that can be invested in a range of assets. No tax will be charged on these accounts at all until your account balance tops €50,000 and, even then, tax will be levied only on any amount above that tax-free threshold.

The tax rate will be 1 per cent. There will be no capital gains tax, no income tax on any dividends or exit tax as applies on similar investment funds.

You can invest €1 or €12,000 in any year and you can invest it all at once or spread it out weekly or monthly across the year. If you do not use the full limit one year, you lose it. You cannot just carry over some of it to increase contributions the following year above €12,000.

There are no restrictions on taking your money out of these accounts either. You can withdraw some or all of your money when it suits you – subject to the limits of the actual investment product you choose.

These is not like the SSIA scheme where the State actually made contributions alongside you to the accounts. Here, the perk is really the fact that the first €50,000 in the account will be tax free.

When will these accounts be available?

Although the details were announced in the budget, they will not be available until July of next year, according to the Minister. This is to allow the Government pass the necessary legislation to set the scheme up and also time for the various investment houses to sort out what options they will offer consumers under the programme.

Who can invest?

Anyone over the age of 18 with a personal public service (PPS) number will be entitled to invest. While it has not yet been made expressly clear, the assumption is that they will have to be tax resident in Ireland.

Each person can have only one account.

There has been some interest from parents in opening these accounts for their children but, for now, no account can be opened in the name of anyone younger than 18. The Minister did hold out the possibility of the scheme being widened down the line to include children but not for now.

Tell me more about how the tax will work

The headline tax rate is very low – just 1 per cent – which certainly makes it sound attractive. However, you are not just taxed on the gains you make in any year but on the total amount in the account above that €50,000 threshold.

Let’s say you have €50,000 in your account at the start of the year and a strong investment return means your account balance rises to €56,000 by the end of the year. The 1 per cent tax is levied on the €6,000 above the €50,000 threshold – a tax bill of €60.

The following year, the investment return is not so good; in fact, your account loses value and by year end is worth €53,000. Even though you have made no money in that year, the 1 per cent tax charge will still apply to the €3,000 in excess of the tax-free threshold, so you will have to pay €30 in tax on an account that lost money.

That will take a bit of getting your head around.

If I’m going to have to worry about Revenue returns and paperwork, I’m not sure I’m interested

Good news, there will be no paperwork and no tax returns – at least not for you. It will be down to whichever fund manager you invest with to make the returns and ensure Revenue gets what it is owed.

Why are they doing this?

The Government is concerned about the amount of “dead money” sitting in bank deposits earning little or nothing. Inflation means this money is actually losing real value every year. The only “winners” are the banks who deposit it with the Central Bank at European Central Bank rates far in excess of what they offer their customers and then use it as a source of “cheap money” to fund their mortgage lending for which they charge you again, boosting their profits every step along the way.

It is also under pressure along with other states across the EU to do more to encourage investment.

If they are so keen to encourage us to invest, why the €12,000 annual limit? Other countries offer far more scope

True, other countries have significantly higher caps on the amount you can invest in such tax-efficient schemes. Why not here? In part, it’s probably a case of taking a fairly cautious approach to a very new type of investment. The Government really isn’t sure how popular this new account will prove to be and they are also wary of people who understand little about investment throwing money at high-risk products only to suffer losses.

And then there are the banks. They are doing very well off this €170 billion on deposit and will no doubt have let the Government know that an exodus of such funds would only lead to higher mortgage costs as banks had to turn to the market to raise funds for lending.

So what interest rate will the new scheme offer?

Now, see, this is the reason everyone is a bit nervous about this scheme.

This is actually one of the questions that was put to our team in the post-budget Q&A. But this is not a scenario where the State is setting an interest rate on your savings. And, in fact, Harris’s team has previously noted that they are not looking at offering the option to invest in cash funds – which are very low risk and operate a bit like a deposit account.

How well a person does under the personal investment account scheme depends on the return on their investment which will be determined by a host of factors – including your choice of investments.

Even with bonds, for instance, which do offer a set interest rate, your return is also determined by the underlying performance of the bond, which can itself rise or fall. You’ll definitely get your interest – unless the bond issuer defaults – but whether you get your original investment in the bond back depends on the market.

Ok, where can the money be invested?

We will get more detail when the legislation is published but what the Minister and his team have said so far is that you will be able to invest in publicly listed company shares, in bonds and in investment funds, including exchange-traded funds – funds that contain a basket of assets that can either mimic a wider index or encourage diversification. These investment funds include those offering exposure to commodities – things like gold or oil.

What will not be permitted is investment in areas of particularly high risk. This includes cryptocurrencies and leveraged investments like derivatives. Areas like private equity and investment in the shares of private companies also seem set to be ruled out.

I know little or nothing about such things. Who will advise me on where to put my money?

You are far from alone. Irish people in general are fairly risk averse when it comes to money, in part because they simply do not understand how markets work. The Government is promising a major financial literacy campaign and the consumer watchdog – the CCPC – has already set up a page to help people understand the concepts around investment. You can find that here. It has also put together a quick online self-assessment quiz with 8 multiple-choice questions to see how ready you might be to consider making investments.

Then, of course, there will be some information provided by the companies that will be selling these investments to you.

I presume they charge for that?

You can expect that they will. Fund managers are going to be keen to keep fees low on the products they sell to people under these personal investment accounts but the lower the charge, the less hand-holding you can expect.

The cheapest (and not necessarily the best) products will offer execution only. That means no guidance or personal interaction with the fund manager. It is up to you to do the homework; they simply sell the product if you decide you want it. The hope is that fees here will be around 0.5 per cent or even less.

If you want a more personal service, you can expect the fee will be higher – closer to 1.5 per cent per annum or more.

So is it a good idea?

Only you can determine if this is right for you. The focus on the Government side is to make these accounts as simple as possible to use. They will certainly offer you the chance to make more than you ever will on deposit but, yes, there is an element of risk involved.

It is not all or nothing; different products will have very different levels of risk. And, over time, such investments have outperformed the return on cash deposits.

As it stands, you are losing money on anything you have on deposit in the bank as inflation is now running at 4.1 per cent, way ahead of any interest you are being offered, even before Dirt is deducted.

You can contact us at OnTheMoney@irishtimes.com with personal finance questions you would like to see us address. If you missed last week’s newsletter, you can read it here.

]]><![CDATA[Never mind the ‘risk to humanity’, Anthropic’s IPO raises more prosaic concerns]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/10/never-mind-the-risk-to-humanity-anthropics-ipo-raises-more-prosaic-concerns/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/10/never-mind-the-risk-to-humanity-anthropics-ipo-raises-more-prosaic-concerns/Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:17:00 +0000Anthropic’s IPO (initial public offering) prospectus warns its AI model could cause a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity”.

Some investors may have more prosaic concerns, not least the amount of new stock coming to market.

Anthropic is expected to make its market debut next month, and it’s already clear that building a $2 trillion AI giant requires a very large cheque.

Revenue rose twelvefold last year to almost $4.6 billion but the company still recorded operating losses of more than $8 billion.

More strikingly, it envisages spending $518 billion on cloud computing and infrastructure in coming years. Extraordinary amounts of capital are therefore needed. Saudi Aramco’s $29 billion flotation in 2019 was the previous record, but SpaceX tripled it in June when it raised $86 billion at a $1.77 trillion valuation.

Now Anthropic will probably blow past even that, with plans to raise up to $100 billion at a valuation of about $2 trillion. And there’s more, with OpenAI expected to follow Anthropic with a trillion-dollar listing in early 2027.

The implications extend beyond the companies themselves. In a recent note, investment manager GMO warned that the sheer amount of new equity coming to market could become a catalyst for an AI bubble break.

For almost all of the past 20 years, US companies have bought back more shares than they issued. That is now going into reverse, with hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Oracle issuing shares to fund AI spending, a wave of giant IPOs adding new stock, and roughly $2 trillion of SpaceX shares becoming freely tradeable by June 2027.

GMO estimates that, if history is any guide, the resulting increase in equity supply could leave the market about 20 per cent below where it otherwise would have been over the following 18 months.

Today’s AI-driven market may therefore face a more prosaic threat than disappointing or even dangerous technology: simply having too much stock coming to market.

]]>Avishag Shaar-Yashuv<![CDATA[Land Development Agency staff share €2m in bonuses]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/10/land-development-agency-pays-out-2m-in-staff-bonuses/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/10/land-development-agency-pays-out-2m-in-staff-bonuses/Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000The Land Development Agency (LDA) paid close to €2 million in bonuses to staff last year, its latest annual report showed.

The State body’s headcount has risen rapidly in recent years as it brought in experienced private-sector staff from firms such as private landlord Ires Reit and homebuilder Evara. Last year, it recruited almost 80 people.

Its annual report said it has put in place a short-term incentive programme (STIP) for staff, which was listed under the organisation’s staff costs. It paid out €1.98 million last year.

The report did not confirm how many LDA staff received a bonus. The LDA employed 250 staff at the end of last year. If the €1.98 million bonus payment were evenly distributed among them, then staff would have received €7,900 each.

Chief executive John Coleman, who was paid a base salary of €200,000, was not paid a bonus in the year. No STIP bonuses were paid to any staff in 2024.

The Irish Times asked the LDA to confirm how many staff were paid a bonus under the incentive programme.

An LDA spokesman said the organisation “competes with private-sector construction industry firms for the experienced staff needed to deliver its large-scale housing programme comprising in excess of 40 projects.

“In order to secure the recruitment and retention of these skills, performance-related awards form part of the agency’s remuneration arrangements, with the exception of the CEO. They are in line with those of other commercial State bodies.”

The LDA was established in 2018 to develop affordable housing on State lands. It has since expanded its remit to partner with developers to help activate private projects to deliver affordable homes.

Coleman, who has led the LDA since it was set up, renewed his contract this year and received a €50,000 increase to his base salary to bring it up to €250,000.

In the past eight years, the LDA has grown to become one of the biggest developers in the State with a total capitalisation potential of €8.75 billion.

It has more than 6,500 homes under construction on about 20 sites. A progress report published in July said the agency would complete 1,800 new homes this year, nearly 3,000 next year and more than 3,500 in 2028.

The annual report showed the LDA’s turnover rose from €78.2 million to €115.9 million last year, with €30.8 million linked to the sale of affordable homes while €23.5 million came from cost-rental revenues.

The agency’s earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) were €6.5 million compared to a loss of €17.5 million the previous year.

In 2025, the LDA made an after-tax loss of €17.2 million, less than the €33 million loss the previous year.

At the end of last year, the LDA controlled €2.5 billion worth of assets, up from €1.4 billion a year earlier, due to the acquisition of new development sites and the completion of many new residential projects it owns and leases to tenants.

The LDA paid €19.3 million in wages to its staff last year, with €2.6 million of this amount paid to the 10-person executive management team and board of directors combined. In 2025, a severance payment was made to one employee, totalling €46,691.

]]>Mark Stedman<![CDATA[Woojer Vest 4 review: This vibrating vest might be the weirdest gadget I’ve ever reviewed ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/consumer-tech/review/2026/10/10/woojer-vest-4-review-this-vibrating-vest-might-be-the-weirdest-gadget-ive-ever-reviewed/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/consumer-tech/review/2026/10/10/woojer-vest-4-review-this-vibrating-vest-might-be-the-weirdest-gadget-ive-ever-reviewed/Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000I have tried out some unusual tech in my time. Bands that tap into nerves to help you lose weight or tackle insomnia. Sensors that encourage you to drink more water. Headphones that also act as a personal air purifier.

But a vibrating vest? That could be the weirdest yet.

The Woojer Vest 4 pitches itself as a “powerful and accurate 360-degree immersive experience”, a similar proposal to the acoustic therapy mat the company makes, but with a different target market. Instead of targeting wellness warriors, the vest is aimed at gamers, movie fans and music lovers who want to feel the audio, although you can use it for meditation too.

The Woojer Vest 4 takes audio and turns it into physical vibration, through six haptic transducers you strap to your body.

It doesn’t matter what the audio is – a movie, a game, Sabrina Carpenter on Spotify – as long as there is a bit of rumble to it. Low-frequency audio rumbles become vibrations and, in theory, you become fully immersed.

Sounds odd? Yes. Did it live up to the promise? Not really.

The device itself looks more like a life jacket than a wellness device or a gaming accessory, but I’ll keep an open mind.

Handily, it comes with instructions printed on the inside. Waist straps get tightened first, then the chest straps, and finally the shoulder straps.

Can a €1,100 high-tech vibrating mat help you sleep?

That was where the first issue became obvious. I’m shorter than average, so the distance between my shoulders and my waist is not quite what it would be for everyone. There isn’t much adjusting I can do on the shoulder straps to get that ideal “snug fit” the vest mentions.

That has knock-on effects. There are two pads on the chest, two on the back and two at the waist. Because of my lack of height, the chest vibration plates are, shall we say, interestingly placed, and the back vibration plates may as well not be there.

To get things working, you need to connect the vest to the Woojer app on your phone.

The unit sent for review needed a firmware update before I could get going, which requires the vest to be plugged in. That led to the second issue: there are two USB ports on the vest, one is on the back and the other on the front left side. Guess which one is for charging? The one I can’t reach without unstrapping the entire vest.

I unhook everything, plug the vest in and get going on the firmware update. Time for problem number three: it fails the first time and takes its time with the second attempt, so I shut it down, reboot the vest and try again. That requires a hard reset (there’s a small pinhole for that).

Ten minutes later we are updated and ready to go. Back on with the straps.

Now you can choose your audio source. The vest will work with everything from iPhone or Android device to PCs, consoles, smart TVs and VR headsets. If it is a phone, tablet or laptop, you can connect via Bluetooth and use either wireless or wired headphones for audio.

Other devices can be hooked up with cables, which effectively tethers you to your seat.

Music is the easiest to test. A wireless connection to the vest, wireless headphones, plus some bass-heavy audio makes for vibration overload. You can dial down the effect either through the app or the physical control panel on the vest. I made the mistake of cranking it up to the highest level on a particularly bass-heavy track and it felt like being hit in the chest. Would I buy a haptic vest for this experience? Unlikely.

Gaming seems like the natural use for the vest. Being able to feel the action instead of just seeing and hearing it would ratchet up the realism.

It didn’t quite work out like that. The haptics are based on audio rather than the game experience. The loudest sound triggers the biggest reaction. If that is the sound effects of the action, great; on some games it was the less crucial background noise, such as the rumble of vehicles and background music.

The problem is that it can all be a bit much after a while. Instead of making you feel more immersed in the content, it can get a bit muddy.

If I am running around a battlefield being shot at, I want the vibration pattern to reflect that. Shot in the chest? The chest plates should vibrate to reflect that. Instead everything blends together, and you can forget the vibration is even there. It is the same for movies and TV shows; sound effects and soundtracks are almost indistinguishable.

Some games have lag when connected to the vest via Bluetooth, even using the dedicated gaming modes. That makes the vibrating sensation distracting rather than immersive because it is coming too late. The settings don’t allow you compensate for it enough, focusing more on audio lag, so your best bet is to use a cable.

The most effective use for the vest is hooking it up to Calm or other meditation apps. But would you spend almost €500 to haul yourself into a vest and vibrate your way to inner calm?

Good

Connects to a range of audio sources, so you have choices about what you want to immerse yourself in. Works well for guided meditation and bass-heavy music, or stealth games that don’t overlay a soundtrack.

Bad

It just doesn’t seem too effective. It works on low-frequency audio – so anywhere there is a rumble, it translates to the vest and the end result isn’t targeted; it just becomes background noise.

The lag on some games devices makes the vest’s effects more of a distractions

Everything else

There are different modes in the app that can help tailor the experience. You can change modes, choosing between broad, focused, gaming and low latency – each has its own strengths. If you are using the vest for gaming, either low latency or gaming mode will be your best bet.

Verdict

The vest makes for an interesting accessory, but it isn’t as effective as I hoped.

]]><![CDATA[Kenmare better off holding out in Irish takeover sweep – for now]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/10/kenmare-resources-oman-abu-dhabi-takeover-mozambique-mine-michael-carvill-tom-hickey/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/10/kenmare-resources-oman-abu-dhabi-takeover-mozambique-mine-michael-carvill-tom-hickey/Sat, 10 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000The United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Oman, which lie on either side of the Strait of Hormuz, have drawn closer since the Iran war began despite reports that some Gulf states privately accuse Muscat of being soft on Tehran as it casts itself as mediator-in-chief.

Most recently, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, UAE’s deputy ruler and overseer of the business interests of Abu Dhabi’s ruling Al Nahyan family, paid a visit to Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said in Oman last week.

The official readout was diplomatically anodyne, citing “strong fraternal ties” and pledging to expand co-operation in the mutual interests of both countries.

While it was unlikely to have featured during the tete-a-tete, a Dublin-listed company has suddenly become an area of common interest: part-owned by Oman’s sovereign wealth fund and, as we learned this week, coveted by a company ultimately controlled by Abu Dhabi’s ruling dynasty.

The Irish Times reported on Tuesday how Kenmare Resources, whose Moma mine in Mozambique produces about 6 per cent of global titanium minerals, had attracted bid interest from Abu Dhabi-based International Resources Holding (IRH).

Kenmare shares soar on confirmation of Abu Dhabi bid approach

IRH, a unit of International Holding Company (IHC), which is chaired by Sheikh Tahnoon, previously ran the rule over Kenmare two years ago, but it came to nothing.

The investment arm of the sultanate of Oman, meanwhile, acquired a 29 per cent stake in Kenmare a decade ago by committing between $100 million (€89 million) and $275 million rescue fundraising, mainly to pay down debt.

While the Oman Investment Authority has been the biggest seller into share buy-backs by Kenmare over the past five years, it retains a stake of more than 17 per cent (held through a vehicle called Africa Acquisitions) and a seat on the board.

That puts the Omanis in a pivotal position should IRH, a mining and trading group, come up with a bid by the November 17th deadline imposed by the Irish Takeover Panel.

It’s hard, however, to see Abu Dhabi coming up with anything near an acceptable price even if Kenmare has become increasingly uninvestable for long-term institutional investors in recent times.

Shares in the company closed on Monday, before news of the non-binding proposal from IRH, at £1.81 apiece. That was 69 per cent below a £5.30-a-share offer made in March last year by Kenmare’s former long-time managing director Michael Carvill and another Abu Dhabi firm, private equity house Oryx Global Partners.

Kenmare rejected that consortium’s proposal as undervaluing the company, but continued talks for more than three months before walking away when Carvill and Oryx indicated they planned to lower their original pitch.

Tom Hickey, who had succeeded Carvill as managing director in August 2024, told The Irish Times in September last year that the exercise was far from futile and had “shone a light” on the fundamental value of Moma – estimated to have a lifespan of another 100 years – even if the price of titanium minerals such as ilmenite, its main product, has fallen sharply in recent years.

But it also served as a reminder that Kenmare is, as Hickey put it, “a small-cap, single-country, single-commodity” company.

Only months after walking away from the Carvill talks, Hickey was forced to take a $301.3 million impairment charge against its Moma assets as Kenmare lowered its long-term revenue assumptions amid uncertainty over pricing.

Ilmenite is now well into its fourth year of decline – driven by Chinese producers, operating at home and in Africa, continuing to oversupply the market. And there’s no sign, as yet, of cyclical recovery. Berenberg analysts recently cut their ilmenite forecasts again and they now reckon it will be 2028 before a recovery occurs.

It’s of minor comfort that the price of zircon, which accounts for about a quarter of Kenmare revenues and is used to make ceramic tiles, has stabilised and is starting to increase again.

The biggest reason stock market investors have been sticking to the sidelines is Kenmare having been in talks for about four years with Mozambican authorities on a key royalties agreement covering Moma. The previous 20-year accord expired just before the end of 2024, though the terms were to remain in place until a new one was reached.

Kenmare, which committed $341 million in recent years on a project to upgrade and relocated its main mining plant in Moma, said in mid-August, as it announced interim results, that it was continuing to “engage constructively” with the Mozambique government and that “significant progress” had been made over summer.

But the longer this drags out, the greater the chances that it ends up in international arbitration.

IRH’s parent, IHC, has a market value of more than €200 billion. The company moved into mining in late 2023 by acquiring Zambia’s Mopani copper operations in a transaction valued at $1.1 billion.

Its mining portfolio grew further last year when it paid $367 million for a 56 per cent controlling stake in Mauritius-based Alphamin Resources, giving it exposure to one of the globe’s largest tin-producing mines in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

IRH’s limited dependence on external debt gives it greater flexibility in financing acquisitions. Its Mopani transaction, for instance, was mainly funded through equity and shareholder loans.

This could allow it to submit a more aggressive offer than a listed mining company or private equity firm could make for Kenmare, both of which might need to secure bank financing to complete a deal.

But would it make a bid before the deadline that’s anywhere near the level that Carvill and Oryx pitched? Unlikely.

Having held out so far, Kenmare may be better served holding its nerve until the ilmenite market at least stabilises and the royalty issue is resolved.

That would offer the best chance of Abu Dhabi putting forward a proposal that its Omani friends – and other big shareholders – would be willing to entertain.

The fifth Irish plc to be subject to a takeover approach this year, Kenmare may be the only one of the quintet to hold on to its independence. For now, at least.

Education

Energy

Q: When does the grant of €600 for solar battery commence?

Pensions

Q: Has a pensioner’s tax free allowance of €18,000 increased?

From Jane

A: Unfortunately, the Government did not announce any changes to the tax-free allowance which currently applies to individuals over the age of 65. – RG

Social Welfare

Q: Will the maternity benefit increase?

A: Maternity benefit is expected to increase in line with increases to social welfare. As such, the weekly rate should increase from €299 per week in 2026 to €309 per week in 2027. – RG

Income Tax

From John Gleeson

A: As a single income married couple, the applicable standard rate threshold should increase from €53,000 to €55,000. – RG

Investment Scheme

Q: Once investments accumulate to above €50,000, it is not clear whether the imposition of a flat rate 1 per cent tax on the value in excess of this is by implication the only tax liability on this value; or if capital gains tax and income tax on dividends is also applied to any gains.

From Nick

A: Based on the documentation issued from the Department of Finance, it would appear that a 1 per cent flat rate of tax will apply to the value of the account above €50,000, but we will need to see the detail in the Finance Bill to understand exactly how the new Investment Accounts will operate. Pensions

Q: I’m a pensioner. My annual total pension is about €22,6450 per annum. Will I be paying less tax next year?

From John

A: You should benefit from some of the tax changes. The exact amount will depend on your personal circumstances.

I have attached a link to the PwC calculator which will give you a better understanding of the tax savings based on your personal circumstances. – BP

Capital Taxes

Q: Regarding childless couples/individuals and inheritance. From Ronan Cull

A: The Group B threshold has increased from €40,000 to €44,000 and the Group C threshold has increased from €20,000 to €22,000. These changes will apply to gifts or inheritances taken on or after October 7th 2026.

Energy

Q: What are the details of the oil boiler replacement scheme?

Pensions

Income Tax

Q: Is the level at which a couple pay the 40 per cent tax rate increased in the budget? I notice there is an increase for a single person.

Energy

Q: Any changes to benefit-in-kind, especially in relation to electric vehicles?

Housing

Q: On mortgage tax relief, will this scheme be offered again in 2027?

Energy

Q: Please explain more about €2,000 grant for replacing old central heating boilers. Can it be replaced by a new and more efficient kerosene fuelled boiler?

Tax

Q: Is there any change to the €3,000 tax free gift amount per year?

Childcare

Social Welfare

Q: When is the increase in fuel allowance coming in?

Childcare

Investment Scheme

Q: Will it be possible to invest the full €12,000 per annum in one go rather than in monthly amounts?

From Marie Porter

A: We’re waiting for the enabling legislation for the fine detail on this but, given that Minister Simon Harris announced an annual contribution limit rather than, say, a monthly limit of €1,000, which would have had the same effect, it seems that you will be able to invest the full €12,000 annual limit in one go rather than drip-fed across the year.

Capital Taxes

Q: Will I get the benefit of the inheritance tax threshold increases for a bequest from a will where the disponer’s death was in early 2026 and the grant of probate was in September 2026?

From James Moore

A: Inheritance tax-free threshold are assessed against date of death, not probate or when the inheritance is received. So, in this case, where the person died earlier this year, it is the pre-budget thresholds that will apply. – DC

]]><![CDATA[There’s a good chance Ireland will come to regret this boomtime period as a missed opportunity]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/09/norway-knows-when-its-tax-windfall-will-end-ireland-doesnt-yet-we-spend-it-anyway/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/09/norway-knows-when-its-tax-windfall-will-end-ireland-doesnt-yet-we-spend-it-anyway/Fri, 09 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000The difference between Ireland and Norway is not just that Norway saves more of its tax windfall, it knows when it will run out.

Geologists can estimate accurately when Norway’s oil and gas reserves will expire.

According to the Norwegian Offshore Directorate, oil and gas production will stay steady until 2030 after which point there will be a steep “tapering off” unless there are new finds.

In Ireland, we have no line of sight. We’re completely in the dark. The tax windfall could go on for another decade or could fall off a cliff tomorrow. Even the chief financial officers of Apple, Microsoft and Eli Lilly, the State’s three biggest taxpayers, don’t know.

And yet we’re funnelling a huge amount of this windfall (€6 out of every €7) into everyday spending, into income tax breaks, into rent supports, stuff that won’t easily be resiled from.

We’re probably the only State in the world that bases its budgetary arithmetic on a handful of multinationals and the revenues they generate outside Ireland.

“The budgetary arithmetic is constructed on the crucial assumption that corporate profitability continues to expand; any decline in profitability could put a (potentially large) dent in corporate tax revenues,” the Department of Finance said in a report released with Budget 2027 on Tuesday.

If we had saved the windfall element of corporation tax since 2015 – approximately 50 per cent of annual receipts – the State would now have a war chest of €130 billion, capable of generating about €10 billion annually in interest (a typical stock market return).

Government ‘will need to borrow’ for new wealth funds as spending rises at fastest rate in EU, says watchdog

This would be enough to do away with the Universal Social Charge (USC) in one fell swoop, without having to raise tax elsewhere.

So much of Ireland’s tax system is still on an emergency setting from the financial crash, USC being the most obvious example.

The tax-free inheritance threshold of €420,000 and the 33 per cent capital acquisitions tax (CAT) that applies thereafter compares with a pre-crash threshold of €542,000 and CAT of 20 per cent.

Of course Ministers will point to the political straitjackets they find themselves in, the realpolitik of a modern democracy.

If Minister for Finance Simon Harris announced this week that he was planning to save €17 billion of the expected €34 billion in corporate tax this year in the midst of a cost-of-living crisis, he would, like Michael Collins, have been signing his own political death warrant and that of Fine Gael.

And therein lies the problem.

Big change requires a break from the sort of electoral budgeting, the winners and losers narrative, that we’ve had to date. A break from the firefighting, from the sticking plaster measures.

We’re apparently rolling in money, but everyone feels poorer and nobody is happy

We’ve had four years of energy credits and we still have the most expensive electricity prices in the European Union (EU). The credits are not a solution so much as a stop-gap. It’s the same with housing. The more money we spend on the housing assistance payment and other rent supports, the more there is a general erosion in affordability.

One senior figure said that Ireland acts like a poor country, spending money as it gets it, gambling on the back of future revenues, when it is actually a rich country that should be thinking more strategically about its wealth.

“Why don’t we feel the budget day numbers? One reason is that it’s going on hiring more staff across the public sector,” he said.

General government spending jumped by 54 per cent between 2019 and 2025, from €86.9 billion to €133.8 billion, facilitated by record corporate tax receipts.

At the same time, employment in the public sector rose by almost 80,000, from 339,000 to 417,000.

“If the Government thinks this (the additional employment) is warranted, it should be paying for it with money it can depend on,” the senior figure said.

Public spending hits record level as watchdog sharply criticises Budget 2027

The Government seems to have shelved any semblance of a plan to widen the tax base and seems content to play the game with the chips it gets from Corporate America.

Experts disagree on whether Ireland has what’s known in economics as “Dutch Disease” – where a sharp increase in wealth in one sector (usually from the discovery of oil or gas) bids up prices, creating cost challenges and a gradual loss of competitiveness.

The National Competitiveness and Productivity Council says Ireland is now “firmly part of the high-cost cluster in Europe”, with labour costs rising faster than the EU average since 2021. In the three years after the pandemic, labour costs rose faster than in the 13 years previous.

After playing a stellar role in financial crisis, Ireland now sits in an ivory tower at one remove from the financial zeitgeist: debt and fiscal constraint.

Tax receipts more than cover spending, resulting in healthy budget surpluses, while Government debt as a percentage of gross domestic product is now under 35 per cent. In the UK (in 2025) the equivalent was 101 per cent. In France, it was 115 per cent. In the US, 121 per cent.

There’s a good chance we’ll come to regret this period as a missed opportunity.

National electricity grid operator EirGrid had four temporary fossil-fuel power plants built in Dublin, Offaly and Kerry in 2023 in a scheme to allow it provide last-resort emergency electricity supplies.

Delays in building new-generation capacity and power lines prompted the energy industry overseer, the Commission for the Regulation of Utilities (CRU), to order recently that the emergency plants remain in place up to February 2029 at a cost of €229 million.

Extending the emergency electricity supply scheme into the next two winters will drive its total cost to €1.44 billion, details published by the commission confirm. Figures from last year showed that its cost had, by then, topped €1 billion.

Homes and businesses ultimately shoulder the cost of maintaining the emergency power plants through network charges on their electricity bills.

Those customers have already paid for their installation, the most expensive element of the scheme, and continue to pay to keep them available.

A CRU note estimates that households could pay between 79 cent and €14.96 a year towards maintaining the backup generators on the system over the next two winters.

How that cost is spread over the years up to 2030 will determine the annual share of the bill paid by residential customers, one industry source familiar with the scheme explained on Wednesday.

EirGrid initially installed the backup plants for three-year terms with optional extensions.

The extensions run to February 2029 in the case of one plant at Huntstown, Co Dublin, and December 2028 for another on North Wall in the capital’s docks. Generators at Shannonbridge, Co Offaly, and Tarbert, Co Kerry, will remain until March 31st, 2028.

Surge in demand for power forces EirGrid to switch on emergency power plant twice

Minister for Climate, Environment and Energy Darragh O’Brien had to approve the extensions given to the facilities before the CRU published its order.

The commission cited delays in building new power stations and in the construction of the Celtic interconnector linking Ireland with France among the reasons for keeping the emergency facilities on the system.

EirGrid has called on the last resort plants only twice since they were built, both occasions this year.

Most recently the grid operator deployed the Tarbert plant for more than an hour after August’s eclipse shut down solar power plants that were then supplying much of the State’s electricity.

EirGrid subsequently confirmed that it used the North Wall facility in June to “manage generation adequacy”.

The grid company always stresses that the emergency power plants are a last resort. EirGrid commissioned them under a plan agreed with the CRU in 2021 to offset the threat of shortages in the Republic’s electricity supplies.

When it comes to the arts, for instance, or newspapers, their views on “fair use” seem firmly rooted in the US legal definition, something that has allowed AI’s scraping of words, sounds and images on a colossal scale without, most of those being scraped would say, anything like commensurate compensation.

Smyth has, she says, strong feelings on the issue. Having studied arts-related areas at the National College of Art and Design, the University of Limerick and the Institute of Arts Design and Technology and chaired the Oireachtas committee on the arts before taking up her current role, she is conscious of the challenges facing those working in the sector while retaining a belief that human creativity will retain a valued edge over that of machines.

“I was out recently in Brussels at a copyright committee, and obviously, as we hold the presidency, we’re very mindful of how we address it. I can’t say I have all the answers on that yet. But I completely understand their desire to protect their original work. It is awful that it would be scraped, copied, plagiarised. What we need to make sure is that they are remunerated correctly for that work.”

Will that happen, though?

“I want to see it happen,” she adds.

The potential impact on the arts touches on the wider potential impact on human engagement and all that entails. The previous day, she says, she was at an event in Maynooth where some big questions were asked, including where this all leaves us as humans.

Smyth readily acknowledges “I don’t have all the answers.”

Beware anyone who says they do.

]]><![CDATA[Jim O’Callaghan dismisses claims of Garda ‘resignation crisis’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/08/ocallaghan-dismisses-claims-of-garda-resignation-crisis/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/08/ocallaghan-dismisses-claims-of-garda-resignation-crisis/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 18:56:06 +0000The strength of the Garda force is about to reach record levels, despite claims for years from the Garda Representative Association (GRA) that resignations and retirements are at crisis levels, Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan has said.

He has also dismissed suggestions the expected all-time peak in Garda numbers, from 14,500 at present to 15,000 in the coming months, will prove very brief and will be almost immediately followed by a surge in age-related retirements that could continue for about a decade.

During that period, according to the Garda’s own projections, the number of gardaí who will reach compulsory retirement age in any one year is set to increase 10-fold.

The GRA, which represents more than 11,000 rank and file gardaí, said while there was provision made in the budget for recruiting up to 1,000 additional gardaí next year, in the first nine months of this year some 400 members had retired or resigned. But O’Callaghan has insisted recruitment is far ahead of retirements or resignations.

“The number of resignations from An Garda Síochána is extraordinarily low, if you look at the PSNI, or any of the police forces in the UK,” O’Callaghan said in a budget event in Dublin on Thursday, insisting that, despite claims to the contrary, the Garda force does not have a resignations problem.

“(Garda resignations) are at about 1 per cent, 140 resignations a year. And, talking to the Garda Commissioner, he tells me that many people who resign come back, and they can be fast-tracked back in.”

He added Garda recruitment was “going well”, with classes of 200 or more now passing out regularly at the Garda College, Templemore, Co Tipperary, and he hoped there could be five such passing out ceremonies per year.

“It’s a great job and a lot of people now realise they want to do a job that doesn’t involve sending and receiving emails all day. And if you become a garda, you’re not doing that,” he said.

Garda retirements set to surge in ‘ticking time-bomb’, projections show

O’Callaghan added retirements from the Garda were “inevitable”. However, he regularly approved extensions of service for members who had reached 62 years, the compulsory age of retirement, but had applied for special permission to continue working for an extra one or two years.

GRA general secretary Ronan Slevin said successive governments had made the same budget promises to increase the Garda by 1,000 members the following year, with minimal impact.

“We presented the Government with a six-point plan suggesting how we could solve a recruitment and retention crisis but have been ignored,” he said.

“We are now on the eve of national pay talks and we still haven’t been told if we will even be in the room when our financial futures are being shaped.

“As of this week, almost 400 gardaí have left the job in 2026 through resignations and retirements, and this number will only get higher by the end of the year.

“The sheer lack of direct engagement by Minister Chambers and his department with the elected members of the GRA has been, for us, disappointing, disingenuous and almost disrespectful.”

The retirement age for Garda members was last year increased from 60 to 62. This had the effect of postponing the start of a projected decade-long retirement spike.

Some gardaí working until age 64 for the first time in history of force

For example, the latest projections by Garda Headquarters show that next year and the year after, the number of Garda members who will reach compulsory retirement age is 37 and 49. However, that is then set to increase every year, for the next decade and will reach 373 by 2035, a ten-fold increase.

Furthermore, the retirement spike will probably start sooner, and worsen more quickly than Garda Headquarters’ projections. This is because the projections are based on all Garda members continuing to work until they are aged 62 years.

In reality, many serving members have a full pension once they reach 30 years service and can retire at any point after they reach the age of 50 years.

]]>Enda O Dowd <![CDATA[Galway bar manager dismissed just 11 days after miscarriage awarded €25,000]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/08/bar-manager-let-go-after-miscarriage-awarded-25000/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/08/bar-manager-let-go-after-miscarriage-awarded-25000/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 16:05:54 +0000A Galway hospitality firm which dismissed a manager just 11 days after she suffered a miscarriage, before trying to claim that maternity protection law didn’t apply since she wasn’t pregnant any longer, has been ordered to pay her €25,000.

Fadeside Ltd, a subsidiary of the Connacht Hospitality Group, has been ordered by the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) to compensate a former manager at its Residence Hotel and 1520 Bar in Galway City for terminating her employment in October 2023 on the stated basis of underperformance.

It is said to be the first time a worker has sought to have the minimum service requirements of the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977 set aside under maternity protection law in the circumstances of a miscarriage.

Normally, an employee requires 12 months’ service before they can pursue a complaint for unfair dismissal – a limitation disapplied in relation to pregnant workers, who are shielded from day one.

The complainant fell ill and was admitted to A&E in September 2023. She found out then that she had been pregnant and was having a miscarriage, she said in evidence to the tribunal.

At the time, she was just under 11 months into a new €60,000-a-year job as general manager at the hotel and bar in Galway’s Latin Quarter.

She said that, after phoning in sick, group HR manager Jackie O’Dowd reached her by phone and said the miscarriage “would make [the complainant] want to have a baby even more”.

At the WRC, O’Dowd denied making the remark.

The complainant said she told O’Dowd in reply that getting pregnant was not something she had planned.

Having returned to work in the first week of October 2023, the worker met her line manager, Wayne Neilon, later telling the WRC she wanted to discuss her working hours and other business maters, she said.

The complainant said Neilon told her she “did not have the core competencies” for the job.

O’Dowd then arrived and asked whether the complainant wanted to resign, remarking that perhaps she “needed a break” because of the miscarriage, the complainant said.

She was told at the meeting that her probation would not be extended and received a letter of dismissal citing “work performance” the following day, the tribunal was told.

The complainant said Neilon had told her months earlier, in May 2023, that she had passed her probation, and that she said so at the October meeting.

In any case, the WRC noted the complainant’s contract capped the maximum probation period at 11 months; by the time of the October meeting, she had 11 months and two days’ service.

The firm’s solicitor, Pat Mullins of O’Flynn Exhams LLP, failed in March of last year in an attempt to have the case thrown out, arguing that enhanced workplace protections under the Maternity Protection Act did not extend to the complainant.

“At the time of the dismissal, the complainant was not, in fact, pregnant, and I say it is a substantial stretch of the interpretation of that part of the Act to state that it includes a previous miscarriage,” Mullins said.

Counsel for the worker, Ian FitzHarris, with Orlaith J Byrne & Co solicitors, said the sacking was just 11 days after the pregnancy loss, his client having worked just five more days after her absence, he said.

“Five days and then they sacked her. The phrase in the legislation is ‘pregnancy-related matters’,” counsel said.

Adjudicator Louise Boyle rejected the respondent’s stance on maternity rights. “It is not in dispute that a miscarriage arises from pregnancy,” she wrote.

“I find that in all the circumstances it lacks credibility that the complainant’s employment was terminated for poor performance,” she wrote.

She concluded the respondent had failed to demonstrate there were the “exceptional circumstances” required to dismiss a worker entitled to maternity protections and awarded €25,000 for unfair dismissal.

Clary<![CDATA[Kingspan faces €40m fine for misleading EU regulators over abandoned deal for Slovenian rival]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/kingspan-faces-40m-fine-over-abandoned-deal-for-slovenian-rival/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/kingspan-faces-40m-fine-over-abandoned-deal-for-slovenian-rival/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 17:16:54 +0000Insulation maker Kingspan faces a €40 million fine for misleading European Commission competition regulators during their investigation of its bid for Slovenian rival, Trimo.

Kingspan ultimately dropped plans to buy the roofing and insulation materials manufacturer in 2022. The planned transaction had triggered a commission investigation into the deal’s potential impact on competition in several insulation panel markets.

The Commission has now fined Kingspan €40 million for providing “incorrect and misleading information” to its review of the Irish group’s bid for Trimo in 2021, a statement said on Thursday.

The Co Cavan-based multinational said it would appeal the ruling.

Kingspan misled the commission on how it tracks the use of mineral fibre sandwich boards, the insulation product made by both companies, against other insulation materials, the statement noted.

The Irish group provided incorrect or misleading information about the availability of bidding data, generally used to assess the competitiveness of a given industry, the Commission said.

It also provided incorrect or misleading information on research and development carried out by Kingspan into mineral fibre sandwich panels.

“This kind of information, which usually only the company itself can provide, is key to understanding a company’s position in the relevant market,” said the commission.

In addition, Kingspan gave incorrect or misleading information about its board members’ involvement in the planned acquisition of Trimo, other deals considered by Kingspan and industry trends and strategy, the commission added.

Kingspan gave the incorrect or misleading information to the commission in either its notification of the proposed acquisition of Trimo or in replies to requests for information under EU merger rules, according to the statement.

The commission has fined Kingspan €10 million for each of the four breaches of merger regulations that it identified.

The EU executive body said it considered Kingspan’s infringements serious as they obstructed the mergers investigation, making it difficult for the commission to properly review the transaction.

“It also considers that Kingspan could not have been unaware of its obligations under the EU merger regulation, meaning that the breach was at least negligent,” the commission said.

“In particular, the commission found that Kingspan asserted the non-existence of key documents, misrepresented facts, or claimed the impossibility to provide key information that only Kingspan was in a position to provide,” it added.

Kingspan responded that it noted the commission’s decision regarding a deal that it ultimately decided not to pursue.

“We look forward to appealing the decision in full,” the Irish group said.

Kingspan did not comment beyond that. But when the commission first questioned the information the company provided to the mergers investigation in March 2024, the group said that it had fully co-operated with the European authorities throughout the Trimo bid.

“This Trimo application was unusual and uniquely onerous given both the level of information sought and the fact that the process occurred during Covid,” Kingspan noted at the time.

“It is in no way representative of the long and productive relationship that Kingspan has with the European Commission.”

Kingspan pointed out that, by March 2024, the Commission had approved four other acquisitions completed by the Irish group since 2020 when it first bid for Trimo.

The European Commission routinely investigates mergers across member states to assess their potential impact on goods and services.

]]><![CDATA[Elon Musk’s ‘X’ loses High Court challenge over Irish regulator’s handling of complaints]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/08/elon-musks-x-loses-high-court-challenge-handling-of-complaints/https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/08/elon-musks-x-loses-high-court-challenge-handling-of-complaints/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 17:26:23 +0000Elon Musk’s X, formerly known as Twitter, has failed in a High Court bid challenging how the Irish media regulator, Comisiún na Meán, deals with user complaints against social media platforms.

On Thursday, Judge Cian Ferriter ruled that the commission is entitled under law to refer information from complaints made under the Digital Services Act to a “supervisory” unit, which also has the power to retain those complaints to identify possible future compliance issues.

X had submitted that the commission could not legally refer information garnered from complaints to the supervision team if those complaints were already concluded or undetermined. They also submitted that information contained within those complaints could not be used for broader, future systemic investigations and that the regulator had therefore acted outside of the law.

X further submitted that it regularly takes “unilateral” removal action, such as in cases of child exploitation, which it is obligated to do by its own regulatory policies. The company submitted that the commission was acting in an “extra statutory” manner.

X had argued that complainants were entitled to an outcome instead of the commission “kicking the can down the road without notification” on any possible future purported breaches.

David Fennelly, senior counsel for the regulator, had said that X was attempting to undermine the watchdog’s important role in cases that had implications across the EU.

The judge said in his judgment that the commission has discretion as to who investigates complaints, adding: “In the circumstances, I do not believe it can be said that the commission improperly disabled itself from exercising its statutory discretion by reference to any of the matters available to it.”

The judge said there was no “improper fettering of discretion involved and no legally impermissible steps on the part of the Commission or its delegates”.

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3444352/">
   <title>Haustiere als US-Konjunkturbarometer</title>
   <description>In keinem anderen Land der Erde leben absolut gesehen so viele Hunde wie in den USA. Der beste Freund des Menschen bekommt allerdings auch dort Konkurrenz: Kurz vor dem Welttag des Hundes am Samstag zeigen nun neue Zahlen, dass sich Katzen heranpirschen. Erstmals seit Beginn der Datenerhebungen leben in US-Haushalten mehr Katzenjunge als Welpen. Laut „Washington Post“ ist das nicht einfach nur ein Modetrend, sondern auch Spiegel der wirtschaftlichen Situation.</description>

Polish prosecutors have asked a court to discontinue a case against three South Asian men who were caught illegally slaughtering a goat at the back of a kebab bar.

They say that the men did not realise they were breaking the law, that such practices are normal in their home countries, and that that the meat was for their own consumption. Prosecutors therefore believe the crime was of low social harm and not worth the court’s time.

🔴Ubili kozę na zapleczu. Wkrótce decyzja sądu, zastanawia ruch prokuratury

Sąd Rejonowy w Wałbrzychu w najbliższym czasie zdecyduje o losie trójki obcokrajowców, którzy pod koniec zeszłego roku niezgodnie z polskim prawem ubili kozę. Oskarżająca Hindusa i dwójkę Bengalczyków…

The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar.

A sign installed to warn the public about damage caused by beavers has been destroyed by the beavers themselves, according to the Polish foresters who erected it.

The incident was reported in a post on social media by the forestry district of Lubliniec in southern Poland, which shared photos of the sign, which read “Warning! Damage caused by beavers”. The wooden post it was displayed on had been destroyed in an apparent beaver attack.

“We wanted to warn you about the potential consequences of beaver activity at the pond and the surrounding area – since beavers dig burrows under the road and fell trees near the pond – but the beavers didn’t want you to be warned, so…they cut down the oak post displaying the hazard notice,” wrote the foresters.

“So, if you are around the pond, please exercise caution; and if you spot a piece of wood sticking out of the ground that has been gnawed by beavers, just imagine there was a sign there reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’.”

Beavers were once almost hunted to extinction in Poland. By 1928, it was estimated that only 235 remained in the country. However, thanks to postwar efforts to reintroduce the animals into the Polish wilderness, the beaver population has grown and is currently estimated at around 150,000.

Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP.

However, the rodents can cause damage to roads, houses and farmland, which has led some to call for culls to keep beaver numbers down.

The Warsaw region, which includes Poland’s capital and its suburbs, had the highest employment rate in the European Union last year, according to new Eurostat data.

The employment rate among people aged 20-64 in the region stood at 86.9%, more than 10 percentage points above the figure for the EU as a whole. It was also the highest recorded for Warsaw since data began to be collected in 2013.

Last year, only four EU regions had employment rates of at least 85%. Warsaw was followed by Prague in the Czech Republic at 86%, Finland’s Åland Islands at 85.5%, and Utrecht in the Netherlands at 85.4%.

The EU average stood at 76.1%, slightly below the target of 78% the bloc set for itself for 2030.

At the other end of the scale, 64 of the EU’s 244 regions had employment rates below 74% last year. The lowest was recorded in France’s overseas departments of Mayotte (36.9%) and French Guiana (50%), followed by Italy’s Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicily (51.4%).

After Warsaw, the second-highest employment rate in Poland was recorded in the central Łódź province (80.8%) while the lowest was in the southeastern Subcarpathian province (73.2%). The figure for the country as a whole was 78.8%, which was only the 13th highest in the EU.

In addition to topping the overall employment rate ranking, Warsaw also had the third lowest rate of youth employment (for people aged 15-29) at 3.9%, higher only than Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (3.8%) and Zeeland in the Netherlands (3.6%).

And it had the third-highest rate of employment among people with tertiary education (93.5%), behind only Portugal’s Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%) and Yugozapaden (93.6%).

Poland's unemployment rate of 2.6% in January is the lowest ever recorded in the country by @EU_Eurostat and was the joint-lowest that month among all EU member states

For more, read our full report here: https://t.co/eP5A9JT4eg pic.twitter.com/A9oHu2zLZ6

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025

The most recent Eurostat figures, from August, show that Poland’s unemployment rate (3.3%) was the second-lowest among all member states and well below the EU-wide figure of 6.2%.

The strong labour market reflects years of economic growth, rising wages and increased employment. However, Poland’s ageing and shrinking population is creating labour shortages and encouraging companies to invest more heavily in automation.

At the same time, job creation is slowing, while some industries – including manufacturing, automotive, furniture and construction materials – are coming under pressure, according to experts.

Ukrainian refugees boosted the size of Poland’s economy by 2.4% last year, the equivalent of 94 billion zloty (€21.5 billion), according to a new report by the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) and accounting firm Deloitte.

The refugees’ level of employment has now also surpassed that of Polish citizens, but their growing presence in the labour market has had no negative impact on employment or wages for other workers, finds the study.

“Refugees from Ukraine in Poland have entered a new phase characterised by deeper economic integration, increasing labour market participation, and a gradual transition from emergency support mechanisms towards long-term integration into public institutions,” wrote the UNHCR and Deloitte.

📉Facts matter.

The findings come in the latest edition of an annual report analysing the economic impact of Ukrainian refugees, almost one million of whom were living in Poland in 2025.

Modelling carried out by Deloitte showed that their presence is having an increasingly positive effect: in 2025, Ukrainian refugees raised Poland’s GDP by 2.4%, compared to 2.3% in 2024, 2.0% in 2022 and 1.5% in 2022. Deloitte forecasts that the figure will rise to 2.8% by 2035 as Ukrainians integrate further.

The company’s latest figures for 2023 and 2024 differ from those published in last year’s report, with Deloitte saying that it now uses a modelling strategy that is “similar to” but “improved” from before.

The report also notes that the figure for 2025 likely understates the economic impact of Ukrainians who arrived in Poland as refugees, given that many – especially the most economically integrated – have shifted from refugee status to other forms of residency, meaning they do not count towards Deloitte’s data.

 

The employment rate among Ukrainian refugees in Poland rose from 61% in 2023 to 76% in 2025. The latter figure was slightly higher than the rate among Polish citizens.

However, the report notes that Ukrainian refugees are far more likely to be employed on a more precarious basis than native workers: only 42% have standard employment contracts, compared to 80% among Polish citizens.

Ukrainian refugees also much more often work in positions they are overqualified for, while their median wage is only around 85% of the figure among all workers in Poland.

Meanwhile, the report finds that, “contrary to concerns that a large increase in labour supply would negatively affect Polish workers, there is no evidence of deterioration in employment outcomes or wages”. In fact, employment among Polish citizens has continued to rise.

The number of foreign workers in Poland rose 7.2% last year to reach 1.14 million.

Immigrants now make up almost 7% of all workers. While Ukrainians remain by far the largest group, the fastest-growing nationalities last year were Colombians and Indians https://t.co/E0LNJXyyTx

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 9, 2026

Through their high levels of employment, Ukrainian refugees also contribute to Poland’s public finances via taxes and social security contributions. The report estimates that general government revenues are 2.6% higher because of refugee-related economic activity.

Meanwhile, although “the arrival of refugees from Ukraine represented a major stress test for the Polish healthcare system…healthcare expenditures on refugees remain substantially lower on a per-capita basis than expenditures on Polish residents”.

Indeed, in 2025, they paid around 2.8 billion zloty more in health-insurance contributions than the cost of the services they received. At the same time, Poland’s understaffed hospitals have been boosted by the arrival of thousands of Ukrainian doctors, dentists, nurses and midwives.

Ukrainians do have access to Polish social benefits, such as grants for children, but these account for only 10% of income in Ukrainian refugee households. The vast majority, 87%, is earned through work.

The research also indicated that Ukrainians contribute between 0.5% and 2.4% to Poland's annual GDP growth https://t.co/KhXxLtif5W

The report notes that the status of Ukrainian refugees in Poland is becoming increasingly normalised, pointing to changes in Polish government policy introduced earlier this year that meant they no longer had special status.
