City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Fri, 09 Oct 2026 21:11:13 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.7 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Where to eat Greek food in central London https://www.cityam.com/where-to-eat-greek-food-in-central-london/ Sat, 10 Oct 2026 09:30:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2464708

If there has been a dominant trend this year with new restaurant openings, it’s the unending rise of the Greek taverna. It feels apt. The same year that pavements cracked with heat and parks turned brittle, a yearning for the Hellenic feels natural. And the Odyssey came out, which felt weirdly foreign in its dark [...]]]>

If there has been a dominant trend this year with new restaurant openings, it’s the unending rise of the Greek taverna. It feels apt. The same year that pavements cracked with heat and parks turned brittle, a yearning for the Hellenic feels natural. And the Odyssey came out, which felt weirdly foreign in its dark dampness this July.

The taverna is a semi chaotic, elbow-pressed testament to grilled meats and oregano-spiked salads. In Athens this summer, I ate bowls of brothy chickpeas at Diporto and in the evening, beef livers and lamb pilaf at Manari Tavern. Back in London, Greek food is hardly groundbreaking, but a new generation of restaurants is very much in vogue. It’s dippier with more bread varietals. The plates and chops are a little smaller, the rooms more contrived in a gesture towards tradition or an attempt at rupture from it. In effect, London-accented. From tasting menus to family favourites, it’s all Greekish in the city.

Oma & Agora

Oma (Michelin-starred upstairs) and Agora (not Michelin-starred downstairs) are two restaurants in the same building in Borough. Set up by David Carter – who recently set up the much-hyped and much-punned Kid – the restaurants are the originators of the new Greek wave. Oma is ‘inspired by the isles of greece’, Agora is ‘inspired by the streets and markets of athens’. Here the emphasis is on flatbreads, dips, sweetly charred skewers and fire cooking. 

Maza

Maza is Mayfair Greek: buzzy and pricey. Tables are pressed together as the well-heeled touch heels. This place has captured the plate-clattering energy of a good taverna, and the taramasalata is pretty perfect too. Owner Christina Mouratoglou says that she wanted to create “fun, warm, organised chaos” when she opened the restaurant earlier this spring as Greek food mainlined into the “mainstream”. Maza ticks those boxes. On the other side of London is Lagana, which opened last year and feels a bit like the Shoreditch crayon-drawn doppelgänger of Maza. Both guarantee a good night out. 

Zylia

Zylia was London’s most hyped opening this year until the next one. It also stirred up a touch of controversy over whether it properly marketed itself as Greek or Cypriot, or a mix of all the food in a palatable jumble of convenience. It’s headed by Nick Molyviatis (family from Athens), an ex-Kiln head chef, and Barry Karacostas (family from Cyprus). As expected from a Kiln alum, the flavour is packing. The milk-fed lamb shoulder is a particular highlight.

Pyro

Another Borough spot, upmarket beach-shack-coded Pyro nods towards the fine-dining end of the spectrum with a tasting menu. Chef Yiannis Mexis, who has worked at Hide and The Ledbury, has created a contemporary, cheffy take on his native cuisine. Some highlights include spanakopita transformed into a Parmesan-dusted nata tart and iberico pork souvlaki. They also serve a room-dividing tzatziki cocktail that tastes just like tzatziki. 

Andy’s Greek Taverna

On the other end of the spectrum is Andy’s with its big ol’ slabs of moussaka and stuffed peppers. A Camden institution serving souvlaki and gyros since the 60s, Andy’s is not the best Greek restaurant in London, but it’s comforting and has one of my favourite restaurant websites of all time (volume up). 

]]> 2464708Carys Sharkey Carys Sharkey Investor pressure mounts on boss of King’s favourite interior designer https://www.cityam.com/pressure-mounts-on-boss-of-king-charles-favourite-interior-designer/ Sat, 10 Oct 2026 04:42:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2464698

A former National Lottery boss is under growing pressure to quit as chair of King Charles’s preferred interior design outlet over opposition to the group’s “lavish” relocation and “poor performance”. Dame Dianne Thompson is facing calls to resign from her role at Sanderson Design Group as part of a campaign against the wallpaper company’s drift [...]]]>

A former National Lottery boss is under growing pressure to quit as chair of King Charles’s preferred interior design outlet over opposition to the group’s “lavish” relocation and “poor performance”.

Dame Dianne Thompson is facing calls to resign from her role at Sanderson Design Group as part of a campaign against the wallpaper company’s drift towards “inaction and inertia”. 

The design group’s history dates back more than a century and its Royal Warrant means the company’s fabrics and wall coverings adorn the official residences of the royal family. In February, the group launched a collection inspired by King Charles’s Highgrove Estate.

LBV Asset Management, which owns about 14 per cent of Sanderson, is pushing for Thompson to be removed as a director and chair. 

“This is by no means an indictment on Dame Thompson’s career or character, both of which are incredibly distinguished,” the investor told Sanderson last month.

“It is an indictment on the current state of the company, which requires leadership – and a chairman – with the mandate and sufficient tenure ahead of him or her to lead a sustained period of change.”

A number of shareholders in the Aim-listed firm, which is due to publish its half-year results on Monday, told City AM that they support LBV’s proposals, voicing a number of concerns over the group’s strategy. 

Paul Hawkins, an asset manager who holds a personal stake in the company, said that Sanderson’s “only excuse for poor performance always seems to come back to difficult economic conditions”. 

“That’s simply not good enough, especially when your biggest competitor in Colefax is performing well,” he added. 

Ex-lottery boss under pressure

Shareholders said that licensing revenue, which grew by a third to £9m in the year to January, is masking the firm’s wider underperformance. 

Hawkins said: “It makes no sense to me why Dame Diane Thompson wouldn’t bow out gracefully and accept it’s time to pass the baton onto someone new with fresh ideas and challenge to a management team that clearly needs it.”

Sanderson is in the midst of a turnaround under chief executive Lisa Montague. The firm posted a £3m pre-tax profit in the year to January, up from a £14m loss the previous year.

But LBV has criticised the board’s decision to approve Montague’s £729,000 pay packet for this year. Her total pay deal, combined with that of Sanderson’s finance chief, accounted to 36 per cent of the group’s profit.

“They are being paid extremely well to repair the profitability that has fallen so considerably under their watch. The Chair doesn’t appear to have a credible answer as to why this is justified,” Hawkins said.

Shareholders expressed concern over Sanderson’s recent relocation to Voysey House, a Grade II-listed building in Chiswick, west London.

One shareholder who is close to the firm’s senior management told City AM that the move to the site of the interior designer’s former factory was a “vanity project” and a “poor use of shareholder funds”.

They said: “Everyone in the industry is at Chelsea Harbour, but Sanderson, at a time of extremely poor performance, decided to relocate to Voysey House.” Another shareholder criticised the “expensive” relocation.

Rhys Summerton, the founder of Milkwood Capital, told City AM that the upgrades to Voysey House ahead of the company’s move were “lavishly done,” though he said it makes sense for the firm to be at its “historical home”. 

A spokesperson for Sanderson said: “Voysey House has been Sanderson Design Group’s spiritual home for more than 100 years. 

“It is central to unlocking the commercial value of our 75,000-piece archive, bringing together our design teams and providing a hub for global customer engagement and partnerships.”

Sanderson ‘neglected by shareholders’

Shareholders said Sanderson has been slow to expand in the US market, where Aim-listed competitor Colefax has toasted an “exceptionally strong sales performance”.

“In my view the business and its leadership need to have much greater focus on their core UK market. They have a wide distribution that they are directly in control of,” the person close to Sanderson’s management said.

“Whilst overseas markets, particularly the US, and licensing are important, they alone will not resolve Sanderson’s problems.”

Summerton said Milkwood has backed LBV’s proposals because Sanderson needs more oversight. “The governance that you see at Sanderson is very similar to the governance that you see at a lot of other smaller companies,” Summerton said.

“Shareholders neglect the company and the decision-making sometimes and the scrutiny of the executives, and that results in underperformance.”

A person close to LBV said that the investor has never taken such direct action with a company before. “They are not an aggressive player in that way but this time they feel they had no choice.”

Sanderson’s history dates back to 1860, when Athur Sanderson & Sons was founded in Islington. In 1940, the designer bought Morris & Co, the brand founded by Arts and Crafts pioneer William Morris. 

The company’s spokesperson added: “The Board firmly believes neither of LBV’s proposed resolutions are in the best interests of the Company and its shareholders. 

“Immediate removal of the Chair would risk unnecessary disruption at a time when the Group’s strategy is delivering measurable progress and profitability, and the Board does not consider that LBV has demonstrated how its nominee’s appointment would strengthen the Company.

“Our focus remains on delivering sustained profitable growth and shareholder value. We will set out our full response to both resolutions in the forthcoming shareholder circular.”

]]> 2464698Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong Bagatelle: Is exclusive Chelsea offering future of Premier League hospitality? https://www.cityam.com/bagatelle-is-exclusive-chelsea-offering-future-of-premier-league-hospitality/ Sat, 10 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2463893

Bagatelle has opened inside Chelsea’s Stamford Bridge. Matt Hardy went down to see if it lives up to its reputation. It feels like every week a top football club opens a new hospitality offering that claims to reinvent what has, in reality, long been the status quo: a good bit of food and a free [...]]]>

Bagatelle has opened inside Chelsea’s Stamford Bridge. Matt Hardy went down to see if it lives up to its reputation.

It feels like every week a top football club opens a new hospitality offering that claims to reinvent what has, in reality, long been the status quo: a good bit of food and a free bar.

That changed, pretty dramatically, when Fulham opened their Riverside Stand with its £20,000 season tickets, Michelin-starred chefs and tidal wave of cocktails.

City AM was told that this offering – seen as one of the best across the Premier League’s 20 clubs – had been topped in another corner of south west London. So, naturally, we had to investigate.

If you were to search for Bagatelle on TikTok just a few months ago you’d have been met with youngsters – 20 to 40 somethings – in Saint-Tropez trying their very best to enjoy themselves in the sweaty French summer.

Do the same search today and you’ll find a very similar clientele – only inside Chelsea’s Stamford Bridge instead.

Bagatelle describes itself as a “French hospitality brand of luxury restaurants and beach clubs”. So why has it gone into football, and why Chelsea?

Bagatelle… at Chelsea?

“Chelsea are world champions, they’re known around the world, they sit in probably the most affluent postcode in sports,” Bagatelle International co-founder Salima Vellani tells City AM.

“Moving into sports was kind of the new flex for us in terms of where the brand is going – it’s more of a luxury lifestyle platform, not just a restaurant group.

“We know where our clients want us to be and so we’re moving in that direction. And sports is missing this layer and it’s never been done in Premier League football.”

The 80-cover offering is, frankly, a little odd. As a sports fan you wouldn’t have known you were at one of the capital’s great sporting arenas. As a Chelsea fan – which the lady next to me was – it may borderline on infuriating.

Getting a ticket at Chelsea is difficult as it is, especially with a number of seats being converted from general admission to hospitality. But Vellani rightly points out that they have instead taken seats away from other premium areas of the ground, rather than general admission.

“I have a brand that I have to protect,” she says. “What I don’t want to do is go in and fit into your box. What I need is [that] you fit into our vision.

“[Chelsea] and Legends, which operates the stadium, are phenomenal partners, they agreed to do it and said, ‘Let’s create something totally different that’s never been seen before’.

“I wanted to create a new category. We’ve been pioneers in the restaurant space, let’s be pioneers in the sports space. I saw a gap, and that gap is luxury VIP hospitality as opposed to what they call premium.”

The reality

What Bagatelle at Stamford Bridge is, however, is perfectly designed for a specific group of people; those who want to experience football their own way. 

Vellani says the offering has been popular with women; at last month’s Hull City game the clientele was predominantly female. 

She says it allows players, their partners and high-level guests to relax. John Terry, harassed for a picture only once or twice, certainly looked at ease.

It has a place in football, and those who hate that may not quite understand how the game has evolved. The food – ranging from tuna tartare to steak to full-time pizzas – was exceptional. The booze – often prescriptive in these settings – was plentiful and wide-ranging.

Bagatelle is known for its party atmosphere, and the Stamford Bridge opening was no different. Waiters stood on chairs singing, lights flickered on, off and on again, and everyone was encouraged to get involved. 

Singing Titanic theme My Heart Will Go On mere minutes before Chelsea saw an early Morgan Rogers goal sunk by two Hull efforts in a 2-2 draw was perhaps not the best example of foreshadowing.

The partnership stems from Chelsea’s deal with Legends – a venue management firm – and Vellani, who said Bagatelle is launching a country club concept and also heading into the boutique hotels market, explains that while this is their first club, it may not be their last.

State of the sport

“We’re partnering with Legends,” she says. “We’re having massive conversations with them and we hope to take this around the world – not only to other clubs in the UK, but the US and further afield. 

“What we don’t want to do is be in a 100 sports stadiums, because that takes away from the brand. We want to be very selective in which ones we go into and Legends are very supportive of that, and actually have recognised that there is a whole new tier of sports hospitality that has gone amiss.

“British sports fans have been very true to the sport. American fans have been very true to the experience and the environment, but Legends have said they haven’t seen this in the US either.”

The reality is the football is changing, fan demands are evolving and clubs are constantly seeking new ways to drive up their top line. That may be an uncomfortable truth for many, but a truth nonetheless.

In Bagatelle’s Stamford Bridge offering – upwards of £1,000 per head – you see hospitality goers turfed out to make room for hospitality goers. It’s like-for-like and that’s perfectly reasonable. 

What you get from the experience, meanwhile, is like nothing else in the Premier League. It’s not premium; it’s luxury. It is finding its place in modern football, and it is, frankly, an exceptional way to spend a couple of hours on a Saturday afternoon.

Andy Burnham’s Downing Street operation has been privately reassuring members of the aviation sector of its support for Heathrow’s third runway expansion, despite the Prime Minister refusing to give the megaproject his backing in a string of media appearances over Labour party conference.

City AM understands that Number 10 has been trying to patch up relations with key figures from the industry after many were left disoriented by the former Manchester mayor’s indifference towards the multibillion-pound drive at his party’s annual jamboree last week. Government advisers have assured the sector that the remarks were not a sign of government going cold on the project, three industry figures said, and that Burnham had not been fully briefed on its economic merits.

“Andy Burnham’s comments weren’t necessarily helpful at the time – but we’ve had some clarification since,” one exec said. “No 10 and internal advisers basically told us the Prime Minister hadn’t really had the time to focus on aviation and the runway. One has to recognise that… his father died [and] he was busy preparing for conference. Aviation was probably the last thing on his mind.”

Proponents of the third runway had initially been encouraged that the change in Prime Minister would not herald any cooling of appetite for the third runway, after Burnham handed aviation minister Keir Mather a brief that explicitly included oversight of Heathrow expansion. Heathrow boss Thomas Woldbye has also said Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, gave the project his blessing when the pair first spoke in July.

Third runway bidders gear up for pivotal evidence session

But their confidence in the project was thrown into disarray when Burnham, who as Manchester mayor called for the third runway plans to be abandoned, told the BBC the expansion was “a matter for London and Londoners”. “I think it’s right that we hear what people have said through the consultation, and then then consider the way forward from there,” he said in an interview ahead of Labour’s conference.

The remarks stood in sharp contrast to the four square support that Keir Starmer gave the runway throughout his time in office. Former chancellor Rachel Reeves made it a central plank of her mission to fire up the UK economy, saying the country could not “duck the decision any longer” in a speech last year that fired the starting gun on its lengthy planning process.

Officials are currently wading their way through responses to a consultation on the Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement, which when published will act as a framework against which bidders’ planning applications will be judged. Civil servants will then unveil a final version of the document, which will be put to a vote now expected in early next year.

Flights by 2039?

If passed, owner Heathrow Airport Limited (HAL) is expected to submit a proposal alongside Heathrow West, a rival bid that is being spearheaded by the billionaire hotel tycoon Surinder Arora. Transport secretary Heidi Alexander will then consider the applications before deciding which, if any, the government should rubber stamp.

But the project has already been dealt its first major blow when HAL conceded it was unlikely to hit its initial 2035 target for flights to take off from the strip. It now expects to deliver the expansion by 2039, assuming the planning process remains on track.

Separately, HAL boss Woldbye and Arora are gearing up for a pivotal evidence session at Transport Committee this week, where MPs are expected to grill the pair on the the merits of expansion and their proposals. Critics argue that even if costs are kept to a minimum, passengers will have to foot the vast majority of the bill via charges that are added to their plane tickets.

A Department for Transport spokeswoman said: “Heathrow expansion has the potential to deliver around £40bn in economic benefits across the UK, and we support airport expansion across the country where this can contribute to growth and opportunity, while meeting tests on the environment.

“We are moving swiftly to review the responses received to the recent consultation on the policy framework underpinning expansion, and considering the appropriate next steps.”

]]> 2464666Ali Lyon Ali Lyon Inherit film review: Thai horror explores society’s Faustian pact https://www.cityam.com/inherit-film-review-thai-horror-explores-societys-faustian-pact/ Fri, 09 Oct 2026 17:33:48 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2464722

Thai horror Inherit skewers youth obsession with slick scares, Buddhist exorcism and a vampish demon grandma; read why its satire endures.]]>

Inherit | Dir. Banjong Pisanthanakun | ★★★★☆

Our obsession with looking – and remaining – young is stretched to its horrifying logical conclusion in slick Thai horror film Inherit. 

The Manasvanich family is in crisis over a chemical leak at their factory, which may or may not be causing birth defects in the local population: the last thing they need is an unexpected visit from a long-lost octogenarian relative. But when Grandma Woranart turns up, she is no little old lady – she’s a bombshell in eveningwear who makes everyone both horny and uncomfortable. 

“Grandma”, as this seemingly twentysomething woman insists on being called, appears to have found the elixir of youth. What’s her secret? Botox? GLP-1s? Chemical peels? Sure, all of those, she says with a sultry smile. The family’s teenage daughter Oui strikes up a particularly firm friendship with Grandma, lounging with her beside the pool and going on girlie shopping trips, only slightly perturbed by the string of violent deaths that follow in her wake.

It doesn’t take long for everyone to realise that Grandma has sold her soul to an ageless centipede demon, and soon the chase is afoot: can the Manasvaniches exorcise this evil spirit before she claims another vessel – and will this secretive family survive intact?

For Western audiences, part of Inherit’s charm is seeing a familiar trope – demons being battled by religious types – shifted to another culture. Priests bearing crucifixes are replaced by robed monks and icons of the Virgin Mary become statues of the Buddha.

Inherit sees Banjong Pisanthanakun on top form

It’s all brilliantly acted, especially the wonderfully over-the-top, vampish performance by Davika Hoorne as the sexy Grandma. It helps that it’s all so gorgeous to look at, with director Banjong Pisanthanakun (The Medium, Shutter) once again showing some exquisite visual flair.

For the first hour, Inherit is content to slowly simmer, demonstrating laudable restraint in the way it dishes out its jump scares and moments of gory body-horror. But the more the net closes around Grandma, the more we see of her true face, and the less frightening the whole thing becomes; a flash of a centipede escaping from under a duvet is a far more chilling sight than dozens of CGI monsters appearing at a window. The introduction of an unlikely deus ex machina to wrap things up in the final act also feels deeply unsatisfying given the solid narrative work up until that point.

Still, Inherit remains a smart and scary satire of our obsession with flawless skin, one that will feel as relevant in Birmingham or Bristol as it will in Bangkok.

Airtel Money chief Ian Ferrao put it best: “when you look at all of the variables, London still comes out top”, writes Lucy Rigby

Reform to strengthen our capital market, making them more dynamic and competitive while preserving the high standards on which their success depends – that’s the change I believe we need to see and it’s the programme I’ve been driving as City Minister. 

Today’s welcome news that Airtel Money has listed on the London Stock Exchange reflects the UK’s status as one of the best places to invest and grow. And I’m determined that this momentum continues.    

The UK brings together businesses and investors from across the world. Our capital markets give companies access to international institutional investors, alongside specialist knowledge of fintech and emerging markets, among many other areas. With more than a third of firms listed on the London Stock Exchange headquartered overseas, the UK’s capital markets have a track record of supporting firms all over the UK, and all over the world, on their growth journeys. 

That combination helps businesses raise the finance they need to grow, while giving investors access to new opportunities. 

But a leading market such as ours cannot rely on its reputation alone. Businesses need a regulatory environment that is rigorous, stable and efficient. The government has undertaken an ambitious programme of reforms to make UK markets more attractive and accessible, while maintaining the high standards that underpin investor confidence.  

The UK’s enduring appeal

Airtel Money’s decision to pursue a London listing is a clear illustration of the UK’s enduring appeal. This business serves more than 53m customers across 13 African countries. They have completed the largest London IPO since 2021. 

The scale of the deal matters. So does the company’s choice of venue. Airtel Money selected London for its access to its deep pool of capital and specialist, expert investors. 

This is not a one-off event. The demand in the market is there, as shown by recent UK listings including Shawbrook Bank, Princes Group, The Beauty Tech Group, Meridian Mining and the National Investment Fund of Uzbekistan. Likewise, the AIM continues to support UK growth companies to meet their needs. Earlier this year, Rosebank Industries raised the largest ever equity placing on AIM, raising over £1.9bn to fund the acquisition of two US industrial businesses. 

A UK listing does not just start and end at the IPO either. The UK is phenomenal at supporting listed companies to continue growing. Over the past five years, over half of the companies listing in London returned to the market to raise additional capital. This far exceeds the rates on the Nasdaq and NYSE, highlighting London’s world-leading support for ongoing capital needs. 

And, as Airtel Money’s chief executive Ian Ferrao said, “when you look at all of the variables, London still comes out top”.   

We have a strong pipeline of talented and innovative companies looking to list thanks to London’s ability to connect high-growth businesses with global investors. 

And we must be clear-eyed: competition between financial centres is real, and companies have choices. The UK must keep making the case through the quality of its markets and the support it offers businesses. That means continuing to improve how companies access capital, maintaining trusted regulation and drawing on the expertise of our financial services sector. 

Airtel Money’s decision is the latest to show that London remains a compelling destination for global companies. Our task is to ensure that the UK continues to earn that confidence. 

Lucy Rigby is economic secretary to the Treasury

Sport seems to increase in popularity year-on-year, and the cachet of attending a major sporting event has never been so high. You may be able to see highlights, clips and chat immediately online, but nothing hits quite like being able to say “I was there”. Other than perhaps being able to remind somebody, “I invited you there”.

The desire to attend and host colleagues and clients at the biggest of games means that some of the mainstream events need to work harder to be the draw they once were. World Rugby has innovated to create the Nations’ Championship and the finals weekend at Twickenham is already proving to be popular with Pitch Experiences in the run-up to the Men’s Rugby World Cup next season. The promise of several matches, northern hemisphere vs southern hemisphere clashes, world ranking points and a trophy at the end of it means that it’s more attractive than the usual autumn internationals series that was played until this season. People want to be part of it and an iconic venue resonates with a global audience.

So we should continue to back our Britishness by going to the best events, whether in the rafters or the padded seats.

Into the Woods by Stephen Sondheim review and star rating: ★★★

Musical theatre can be self-referential, didn’t you know? Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine certainly do. Their Into The Woods maxes out on meta gameplay in this technically brilliant but at times baseless musical that can be terribly proud of itself.

A baker and his wife plunge into Tom Scutt’s endless-feeling set, which is in effect a handful of trees and some carefully placed reeds but feels immensely lush and escapist, in order to break the spell that forbids them from having children. They must venture into the woods to bring back four items: a cow as white as milk, a cape as red as blood, hair as yellow as corn, and a slipper as pure as gold, says a familiar-looking witch, and Cinderella, Little Red Riding Hood, Jack from Jack and the Beanstalk are along for the ride too (don’t ask). 

Into the Woods: London return is technically spectacular

As for the music, it’s no surprise that Cinderella and Little Red Riding Hood have whooping great belts; it’s all technically spectacular and the music relieving because, frankly, Lapine’s script is often mercilessly verbose, overflowing with narrative information about the side quests of each of the characters. By the end of the first act it appears to be a fun, big-hearted journey, and musically triumphant, and everyone gets what they wish for, babies are due and it’s all gravy – but there is a second act in which everything falls apart again when a new plot is introduced: a vengeful giant is on the loose.

I’d imagine the Venn diagram of Stephen Sondheim and Brothers Grimm fans is fairly robust, but the conceit starts to feel like intellectual masturbation by the second act. After all, the viewer has no cliffhanger to resolve after the interval, which itself feels longer than other shows (I don’t know if this was intentional, or if there was a production issue on the night I went in). Anyway, returning to my seat after a lengthy first act, and due to the fast-paced, sometimes overwhelming narrative, I was wearying of this forest-dwelling gang, a feeling I found hard to shake even with the arrival of the eventual fee-fi-fo-fum thuds of the worrisome vertically accomplished beast edging ever closer.

Tunes aren’t gripping

The other problem with Into the Woods is that there’s a lack of conventionally melodic pop songs to tide you over. The main refrain – into the wooooooodsssssss – is repeated a thousand times, and is unconventionally catchy, but not in the rewarding way of something more tuneful. The metaness bleeds through from the staging into the ballads: everyone’s belting something for the sake of musical theatre, darling, but perhaps when everyone’s belting, no one’s belting at all. 

I don’t want to diminish the innovative brilliance of this expansive idea, which genuinely transports you somewhere fairytale-coded and magical looking. Call me Scrooge (one of a  few fictional characters who doesn’t get a look in) but I suppose you could argue that the virtue of fairy tales is that they end quickly. There is energy and wonder here, though I left a little exhausted.

Into the Woods plays at the Noël Coward Theatre until 9 January 2027

Retaining the individuals who allocate capital and fund business expansion should be considered a national priority, but Healey looks more likely to drive them away, writes Tom Goddard

Financial professionals have the resources to leave the UK if they feel unfairly targeted by tax rises, or that the tax they pay is not spent wisely by the government. By increasing taxes such as Capital Gains Tax (CGT) or dividend tax in the Autumn Budget, the Chancellor John Healey could be sacrificing long-term, high-value tax contributions for a short-term fiscal gain.

The top 10 per cent of taxpayers in the UK contribute 60 per cent of total income tax receipts. Private equity houses and venture capital firms directly generate approximately £200bn of the UK’s GDP, representing around seven per cent of economic output, and support more than 2.5m jobs, all of whom will pay income tax and National Insurance Contributions (NICs).

London remains one of the world’s premier financial centres. Alongside New York, it is one of only a handful of genuinely global hubs for financial services, private capital and asset management. It possesses a unique ecosystem comprising world-class legal services, deep capital markets, leading universities, a highly skilled workforce and an abundance of financial expertise. The government should recognise this as a national strength that can attract and retain global talent and focus on promoting its growth rather than treating it as a bottomless well for ever-higher taxation.

Healey must think longer term

When senior investment professionals choose to locate in London, they bring with them whole networks of advisers and businesses. They deploy capital into British businesses, support entrepreneurial ventures and create opportunities for future generations of founders and employees. The compounding effect generated by these industries has helped make London Europe’s dominant financial centre, which ultimately leads to larger tax hauls.

The danger is that when a senior financial executive relocates away from the UK, this wider supporting network of professionals may also leave. Although London’s success as a financial hub is not based on the UK’s tax regime, it is not immune from competition from other jurisdictions able to capitalise on the flow of professionals and businesses from the UK, which eventually, may weaken the same ecosystem that made the UK attractive in the first place.

Healey’s approach should therefore be one of strategic competitiveness and continued growth. Rather than viewing successful investors and entrepreneurs primarily as a source of additional tax revenue, the government should recognise them as drivers of economic activity whose presence generates investment, employment and innovation throughout the wider economy.

The UK is in competition with several countries that are actively seeking to attract internationally mobile wealth creators through favourable tax regimes. Greece, Italy, Portugal, Switzerland and the UAE have all developed frameworks designed to appeal to entrepreneurs, investors and senior financial executives. Their objective is to attract high earners who generate tax revenue, invest capital, create jobs and support economic growth.

At a time when economic growth remains the government’s primary challenge, retaining the individuals who allocate capital and fund business expansion should be considered a national priority and the UK must ensure that it remains not only a great place to invest, but also a great place for investors to live, work and build their businesses.

Tom Goddard is an assistant manager at Blick Rothenberg

You know something is wrong with the upper end of Britain’s labour market when some of the country’s most promising companies find it is easier to relocate top talent from America than hire from our own shores.

But those are exactly the lengths to which one founder told me he and his fellow UK tech entrepreneurs are regularly going to take on high-skilled engineers quick enough to fuel their companies’ rapid growth.

The rise in this sub-optimal practice is not, you will be relieved to read, for a lack of high-functioning, high-IQ minds being churned out by our universities.

I make no apologies when I say that the issue of excessively long non-competes has become something of a cause celebre for City AM over the past few months.

But one bright pocket where we can go toe-to-toe against pretty much anyone is… brains. Few places, if anywhere, can lay claim to the volume of scarily clever people that currently reside in the ‘golden triangle’ between London, Oxford and Cambridge.

Rent musical review and star rating: ★★★

It’s pertinently ironic that Rent’s press night coincided with the London Film Festival premiere of Elsinore, Andrew Scott’s remarkably tender AIDS drama. Perhaps in the late-eighties when this musical was conceived, even talking about the epidemic on a stage was politically powerful, even if it were sprinkled as a theme rather than addressed head-on like dramas do today. 

By those standards, Jonathan Larson’s Rent, which follows a group of creatives fighting eviction from their New York building, was once fearsomely progressive. But by today’s standards, taking something so horrific as AIDS, which took the lives of 20,000 Brits alone, and putting it as a backdrop to a central story about people getting kicked out of their flats (which is dealt with with far more emotion) feels strange and tone deaf.

Rent musical: go for the music

In act 2 there is one attempt to go beyond two-dimensional representation with the platforming of the death of one character, Angel, to the disease, which is treated with more sensitivity via the track I’ll Cover You, but this production lets down the attempt: dressed in y-fronts and disappearing within sheets, Angel’s death feels bizarre and emotionless rather than profound.

Regardless, the pop-rock songs are fun, most notably Seasons of Love, famous more recently from Glee, even if many are strangely buoyant given they’re often about dying and how many of the characters have the disease.

If Rent is for one thing, it is taking in these spectacular songbooks, which includes bangers like La Vie Bohème, One Song Glory and Take Me Or Leave Me. Olivier Award-winner Luke Sheppard’s conventional production doesn’t play much with the formula; David Woodhead’s set is similarly predictable, centring upon a shabby-looking apartment.

Huge fan clout

Beyond that though, the story line often there to service the arrival of the next song rather than advancing the plot, especially when central character Mimi is about to die from AIDS related conditions but is saved when her partner Doug walks in and apparently sings her back to life, which feels problematic in just about every way possible.

Anyway, who cares what I think, Rent holds huge fan clout. Sit back and listen to the music and you’ll have a nice time. 

Rent plays at The Tom Stoppard Theatre until 29 May 2027

A former City trader previously convicted of rigging the Euribor interest rates has had his fraud conviction overturned.

Christian Bittar, formerly a trader at Deutsche Bank, had his conviction overturned by the Court of Appeal on Friday after being sentenced to five years in prison for rigging the primary European interest rate, the Euro Interbank Offered Rate (Euribor), in the run-up to the financial crisis. He previously pleaded guilty to the charge.

“For reasons we will set out at a later date, this conviction has been quashed,” Lord Justice Edis told the court.

The decision comes just over a year after the Supreme Court’s landmark decision to overturn a similar ruling on former UBS trader Tom Hayes and Carlo Palombo, formerly of Barclays, last year, after finding they had been “deprived” of a fair trial as the judges had given “inaccurate and unfair” directions to the juries which found the traders guilty.

The two former City traders became the faces of the so-called ‘Libor scandal’ which saw the Serious Fraud Office (SFO) pursue a volley of prosecutions in the wake of the 2008 crash.

However, in Bittar’s appeal, he claimed he had pleaded guilty on the wrong legal basis, and brought his appeal after the Supreme Court overturned Hayes’ and Palombo’s convictions.

Speaking after the hearing, Hayes told City AM: “I’m overwhelmed because it’s been a long, long journey, and I’ve been fighting for all of us, not just me.

“The fact that now somebody who pleaded guilty has had their conviction deemed unsafe by the Court of Appeal is a huge step towards correcting all the injustices that took place in this series of cases,” he added.

The latest decision comes after five former City traders, Jay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon and Colin Bermingham, previously convicted of rigging the Libor (London Interbank Offered Rate) and Euribor interest rates had their fraud convictions overturned by the Court of Appeal on Wednesday, all of whom pleaded not guilty.

The five investment bankers, who previously worked at Barclays, had their convictions quashed having served jail-time for conspiring to rig the now-defunct Libor interest rates in the run-up to the financial crisis.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) referred the cases to the court in January after the fraud watchdog, which brought the prosecutions over a decade ago, said it would not seek a retrial against Hayes and Palombo.

“I have waited a very, very long time for this day. Finally, the injustice of what I and others suffered has been recognised. I am so grateful for those who stood by me through this ordeal and those who worked so tirelessly to correct it,” Bittar commented after the hearing.

Ben Rose, of Hickman and Rose, representing Bittar, said it “is significant that the Court of Appeal today quashed Christian’s conviction in face of opposition from the SFO.” 

“The decision to quash Christian’s guilty plea illustrates the severity of the injustice he suffered. Courts are naturally reluctant to set aside guilty pleas, so I am delighted that the Court of Appeal agreed that, exceptionally, it should do so in this case,” Rose said.

“It is a scandal that the SFO has consistently failed to uphold its duty to seek to ensure that these trials are fair. It is hard to see how it will learn the lessons it needs to of this saga until it accepts it was wrong,” he said.

‘The last chapter’ in the rates-rigging scandal

Bittar is the last of the group of former traders who have had their appeals heard.

“Some of us lived that history. It’s quite something to be here today in the last chapter of it,” Bittar’s barrister told the court.

However, the ninth and last former trader who was pursued by the SFO, Peter Johnson, formerly of Barclays and the original whistleblower in the rates-rigging scandal, is in the early stages of an appeal, Lord Justice Edis confirmed to the court on Friday. Like Bittar, Johnson also pled guilty, and was sentenced to four years in prison.

“The quashing of these convictions is welcome news and another important step on the way to correcting this terrible miscarriage of justice,” Ellen Gallagher, partner at Vardags, who represents Johnson, said. 

“But Peter’s fight to clear his name continues, and he intends to appeal. As the Court made clear today, he has taken the first steps towards that appeal by filing provisional grounds. 

“We await the Court’s fully reasoned decision on this week’s appeals and are considering next steps,” Gallagher said.

As David Cameron turns 60, Eliot Wilson takes a look back at the life so far of the “chillaxed” Prime Minister

Last Tuesday, while Andy Burnham was addressing the Labour Party’s annual conference for the first time as Prime Minister, there may have been a brief but smooth, refined cry of anguish heard above the slates of West Oxfordshire.

“Brexit has done more harm than good. We need to restore a higher level of growth and prosperity for Britain.”

Lord Cameron of Chipping Norton allowed the Brexit referendum of June 2016, campaigned for the United Kingdom to remain within a reformed European Union and, when the electorate voted by 52 per cent to 48 per cent to leave, resigned. He might have thought: yes, that’s what I said, that was my whole point.

A silver spoon childhood

David William Donald Cameron was born on this day 60 years ago in Marylebone, the third child of stockbroker Ian Cameron and Mary Fleur Mount, a Justice of the Peace. His was an upper-class childhood with which older generations of Tories would have been entirely familiar. The country estate in Aberdeenshire, Blairmore House, built by a great-great-grandfather who had made his fortune in Chicago’s grain trade, was sold just after Ian Cameron was born.

David was raised in Berkshire, and followed the well-trodden cursus honorum of Heatherdown School and Eton. His schooldays are telling. He was academically extremely able, but conventional. Caught smoking cannabis six weeks before his O-levels, he was reprimanded and gated rather than expelled, as he had only been consuming, not selling. Unlike his brother Alexander, Cameron was not elected to the Eton Society, or “Pop”.

Fellow Etonians seem to agree that Cameron was amiable, amusing – and forgettable. He passed the Oxford entrance and won an exhibition to Brasenose College, to read the ubiquitous philosophy, politics and economics degree.

PPE had started at Oxford in 1921 and in Cameron’s day still had the lustre of “modern Greats”. It had produced heavyweight figures on the left
(Harold Wilson, Roy Jenkins, Anthony Crosland, Barbara Castle) and the right (Edward Heath, Michael Heseltine, Nigel Lawson, Australian PM Malcolm Fraser).

A subtle shift seems to have occurred in his life at Oxford. He spent a gap year working first for a Conservative MP then at venerable conglomerate Jardine Matheson in Hong Kong, and when he went up to Brasenose, Cameron, never flappable, found a new level of reassurance.

He was no longer the amiable but anonymous figure of Eton. As a politician he would focus on pragmatism and practicality; as an undergraduate Cameron was widely reckoned to be extremely able. His economics tutor recalled, “We’ve had rather few Prime Ministers who’ve been as intellectually able as David”; his politics tutor Sir Vernon Bogdanor described him as “one of the ablest” students he had taught.

Guy Spier, who shared tutorials with Cameron and went on to consultancy and investment banking, was daunted by the way Cameron thought.

“We were doing our best to grasp basic economic concepts. David – there was nobody else who came even close. He would be integrating them with the way the British political system is put together.”

Socially Cameron’s polish may have outrun his judgement: he joined the all-male dining society the Bullingdon Club, notorious for alcoholic excess and reckless property damage. Even there, his noticeable poise attracted attention. David Worth, an American postgraduate invited to join, remembered “a surreal Brideshead Regurgitated quality” to the club; but he remembered Cameron extensively quoting Winston Churchill from memory. “He was very funny… articulate and lucid… the centre of attention”.

Cameron avoided student politics; perhaps that was why as a politician he was able to seem a fraction more normal than colleagues. This was a rich period at Oxford, the political stage graced by Boris Johnson, Michael Gove, David Miliband, Jeremy Hunt, Ed Balls, Frank Luntz, Ed Llewellyn, Ed Vaizey and Radosław Sikorski.

The political years

He was not hobbled by avoidance. A few months after graduating, Cameron joined the Conservative Research Department, as did his Eton friend and future chief of staff Ed Llewellyn. He stayed for five years and this time he did mingle with young and ambitious Conservatives like Vaizey, Llewellyn, Kate Fall and future husband-and-wife Rachel Whetstone and Steve Hilton.

Politics was life at full pelt. In 1991 Cameron was seconded to 10 Downing Street to help John Major prepare for Prime Minister’s Questions (then held twice a week) and is credited with polishing the premier’s performances. He missed out on the position of political secretary to the PM but was part of the “brat pack” working 20-hour days on the 1992 general election campaign: against expectation, the Conservatives won.

Cameron’s reward was to be special adviser to Chancellor Norman Lamont. On a family holiday that summer in Italy, he began a relationship with a friend of his sister Clare, Samatha Sheffield, an aristocratic, Bohemian art student of 21 – they married four years later. Cameron returned to his post just in time for Black Wednesday, 16 September 1993, when sterling plummeted and Lamont had to withdraw the UK from the Exchange Rate Mechanism.

The punishing grind of the 1992 general election reportedly made Cameron resolve to exchange politics for journalism. Somehow it never happened. He would step back for a few years to Carlton Communications, but was selected as candidate for Witney in Oxfordshire in 2000; the sitting MP, his old Conservative headquarters colleague Shaun Woodward, had defected to Labour. Cameron was elected in 2001 and spent 15 years as a member of Parliament. 

It is a modest enough length of service, but Cameron always packed these things in: MP at 34, frontbencher at 36, shadow cabinet at 37, party leader at 38. By the time he resigned as Prime Minister in 2016, Cameron was still in his forties.

The ‘chillaxed’ politician

There would be a short Indian summer: in November 2023, Rishi Sunak surprised Westminster by appointing Cameron as foreign secretary in the House of Lords. He was the seventh former Prime Minister or party leader to take the post, and although he was only in office for eight months, his presence brought a degree of calm and reassurance to a fractious and exhausted party. Lord Cameron, as he became, was a grown-up.

It was a sense of poise which defined David Cameron, for good or bad. Some called it entitlement or arrogance, and he never denied being a product of privilege. But an otherwise happy upbringing and life had been severely tested: his father Ian had been born with both legs severely deformed, requiring repeated surgery as a child and eventually double amputation.

And David and Samantha Cameron’s eldest child, Ivan, suffered from Ohtahara syndrome, frequent seizures necessitating constant care from clinicians and family. There was an unforced authenticity to Cameron when he spoke of the human side of the NHS and the emotional weight of parenting. But he was able to look inward to his family to sustain him.

There is value in a leader who has not sought office out of a sense of manifest destiny, like Tony Blair, driven by deep-seated internal psychodrama – Gordon Brown or Boris Johnson – or chasing implacable ambition, like Liz Truss. Cameron, from his schooldays, assumed that a successful political career was open to him, and that was the path he chose.

But it need not have been, and even the premiership did not devour him. An unnamed colleague once sniped, “If there was an Olympic gold medal for ‘chillaxing’, the Prime Minister would win it”. This suggested constant prostration from exhaustion and anxiety were recommendations in a leader.

When Earl Grey resigned as Prime Minster, William IV invited the home secretary, Viscount Melbourne, to form a government. Melbourne told his private secretary, Tom Young, “I think it’s a damned bore. I am in many minds as to what to do.”

Young’s response was stern: “Why, damn it all, such a position was never held by any Greek or Roman: and if it only lasts three months, it will be worthwhile to have been Prime Minister of England.”

Cameron, a descendant of William IV, had something of the spirit of Melbourne (an Etonian who had a disabled son). He was ambitious but office did not obsess him. Perhaps the most eloquent expression of his inner calm, his willingness to take each day as it came, was unwittingly captured on microphone as he gave his farewell speech outside 10 Downing Street on 13 July 2016.

“Thank you very much. [Walking away] Doo, doo, doo, doo. Right.”

Eliot Wilson is a writer and historian. He is a senior fellow for national security at the Coalition for Global Prosperity and a contributing editor at Defence on the Brink

The XPeng G6 undercuts BMW’s iX3, Audi’s Q6 e-tron and the electric Mercedes GLC by around £20,000, and charges faster than all of them. So what does the German badge actually buy you?

For years, buying a premium SUV meant picking between three German badges. BMW, Audi and Mercedes still own that conversation, but the XPeng G6 is making a decent case that the badge has become the most expensive option on the spec sheet.

XPeng is a Chinese brand that has only been on sale in the UK since 2024, although the UK-spec G6 is assembled in Graz, Austria, by Magna Steyr, the same contract manufacturer that builds the Mercedes G-Class. That’s worth knowing before you file it away under “cheap Chinese EV”.

XPeng G6 price vs BMW iX3, Audi Q6 e-tron and Mercedes GLC

The G6 range runs from £39,990 for the Standard Range, through £44,990 for the Long Range, to £49,990 for the Performance model.

The fair comparison is with the electric versions of the German cars, and the gap there is wide. BMW’s iX3 starts at £58,755, the Audi Q6 e-tron at £60,565 and the electric Mercedes GLC at just over £60,000, which means even the range-topping G6 Performance comes in around £9,000 under the cheapest of them.

There’s a tax angle here too, and it’s one I’d want any buyer to clock. Since April, electric cars only pay the Expensive Car Supplement if their list price tops £50,000, and every G6 sneaks under that line as long as you go easy on the options, while all three German rivals sit above it. That adds up to £440 a year, for five years, that a G6 owner simply doesn’t pay.

XPeng G6 range and charging

Range is where the Germans fight back. The G6 Long Range claims up to 326 miles, against up to 393 miles for the Audi Q6 e-tron, 406 for the electric GLC and 500 for the BMW iX3, so if you regularly cover big motorway distances without stopping, that gap is a real consideration.

Charging is where the G6 wins it back, and then some. The Long Range and Performance models charge at up to 451kW, which XPeng says takes you from 10 to 80 per cent in around 12 minutes on the right charger, quicker than any of its German rivals, the iX3 included.

There aren’t many public chargers that can deliver those speeds yet, so treat 12 minutes as a best case. But if you do most of your charging at home and only top up on longer trips, I’d take faster charging over an extra 70 miles of range every time, because a 12-minute stop fits around a coffee while a 40-minute one starts eating into your afternoon.

XPeng G6 interior and technology

The G6 was updated for 2026 with what XPeng says are more than 20,000 engineering changes, including revisions to the suspension, steering and motors aimed at making it better to drive.

Inside, you get a 15.6-inch central screen, wireless phone charging at up to 50W, a suede-effect headlining, wood-grain dash trim and rear seats that recline. XPeng has kept physical stalks and steering wheel buttons for the essentials, although the rest of the dashboard is almost button-free, and Carwow found navigating the menus for everyday functions irritating even if the software itself is slick.

Practicality is mostly good, with a 571-litre boot that’s bigger on paper than the electric GLC’s 520 litres. It is shallow, though, so taller items can block the rear window, and there’s no front boot for stashing cables.

Is the XPeng G6 as good as BMW, Audi and Mercedes?

The Germans do still earn some of their premium. BMW’s iX3 was named World Car of the Year for 2026 and has far more range, the electric GLC leans hard into comfort and cabin quality, and all three come with established dealer networks and a familiar ownership experience.

That last point is the G6’s biggest weakness, because XPeng’s UK dealer coverage is still very limited and servicing could mean a longer drive than you’d like. There’s also no long-term used market yet to tell you what a three-year-old G6 is worth, and on a car bought on finance, the residual value has a big say in your monthly payment. The styling is fairly anonymous too, which may or may not bother you.

XPeng G6 verdict

On the numbers, the G6 wins by some distance. It’s around £20,000 cheaper to buy, it dodges a tax the Germans all pay and it charges faster than any of them, so if you’re spending your own money and you’re comfortable being early to a brand, the Long Range at £44,990 is the one I’d look at hardest.

Where the Germans still justify the extra is everything around the car, from dealer coverage and a known resale value to a badge your clients will recognise. For some buyers that’s worth £20,000, but I suspect that for a growing number, it won’t be.

It was Britain’s best-selling car in both 2023 and 2024, and it topped the charts again in August, despite an avalanche of new small SUVs and electric crossovers chasing exactly the same buyers.

The basic recipe is a simple one. You sit higher than you would in a hatchback, which makes getting in and out easier and gives you a better view in traffic, while the car itself stays compact enough to park without needing a second attempt.

Volkswagen is retiring the ID.4 and putting its best-selling SUV name on the replacement. Early prototype drives suggest it’s quieter and comfier, but the charging hasn’t moved on as much as it should have.

Volkswagen’s ID naming never quite stuck with buyers, and the company seems to have admitted as much. The ID.2 became the ID. Polo, and now the ID.4 is being replaced by the ID. Tiguan, borrowing the name of one of the most popular cars VW makes. Tiguan and Tayron deliveries passed a million globally last year, so if you’ve got a badge people already trust, putting it on the electric version is a sensible bit of business.

The ID.4 and its coupe sibling, the ID.5, have sold more than 950,000 between them since 2021. That’s a decent result, but the name never meant much to anyone outside the car industry. “Tiguan” does.

The full reveal is due in early October, with the car going on sale in 2027. A handful of outlets have already driven late-stage prototypes, and the early picture is a family SUV that’s been refined more than reinvented.

What’s the Volkswagen ID. Tiguan like to drive?

Top Gear drove a camouflaged prototype on roads near Vienna and found it quieter, comfier and plusher than the ID.4, with the ride staying settled on 21-inch wheels and the steering unbothered by potholes. WardsAuto came away with much the same impression, describing a car built around comfort and ease of driving, with no attempt to turn it into a sports SUV.

That sounds like the right call to me. Nobody buys a mid-size electric family SUV to chase apexes, and the ID.4’s weak spot was always refinement. It felt a bit cheap and a bit noisy for the money, and that’s exactly what VW appears to have worked on.

Not every early drive was glowing, though. Auto Express tried an earlier prototype last year and felt it wasn’t drastically different from the ID.4 on the road, although that drive was over smooth tarmac that didn’t ask much of the suspension.

Volkswagen ID. Tiguan battery, range and charging

There will be two batteries. The smaller 58kWh lithium iron phosphate pack is expected to manage around 280 miles, while the 77kWh nickel manganese cobalt battery in the Pro and Pro 4Motion versions stretches to a claimed 373 miles in the rear-drive Pro. That’s a small step on from the ID.4’s 351 miles, competitive for the class without leading it.

Charging is where I’d have liked more. Peak rates are reported at 105kW for the smaller battery and 165kW for the larger one, the same as the ID.4, which works out at roughly 26 and 29 minutes for a 10 to 80 per cent top-up. That’s perfectly usable, but the Tesla Model Y and several of the new Chinese rivals charge faster, and a replacement model was the obvious moment to catch up. Every version does get 11kW home charging, plus vehicle-to-load through VW’s PowerSocket adaptor, so you can run a kettle or a laptop off the battery.

Volkswagen ID. Tiguan power and performance

Power outputs carry over from the ID.4. The 58kWh rear-drive model makes 188bhp, the 77kWh rear-drive Pro gets 282bhp, and the dual-motor Pro 4Motion tops the range with 295bhp and four-wheel drive.

Volkswagen hasn’t published acceleration figures yet, and Top Gear’s seat-of-the-pants estimate for the Pro was around seven seconds to 62mph. Brisk enough for a family car, and in line with the brief. The 4Motion makes most sense if you deal with slippery roads regularly or need to tow, with a towing limit of up to 2,000kg expected, handy if there’s a caravan in the picture.

Volkswagen ID. Tiguan interior and boot space

The prototypes had their dashboards covered, so the full picture will have to wait for October. What is visible is a bar of physical buttons similar to the one in the ID. Polo, proper controls back on the steering wheel and a large central screen sitting on top of the dash. Anyone who spent time jabbing at the ID.4’s touch-sensitive sliders will be glad to see real buttons return.

The ID. Tiguan is around 44mm longer than the car it replaces, and there looks to be more space in the back, plus a front storage compartment for cables. Volkswagen hasn’t released boot figures yet. Production will be at VW’s Emden plant in Germany.

Volkswagen ID. Tiguan UK price and on-sale date

The reveal is due in early October, with UK pricing and specification to follow and cars arriving in 2027. Britain is expected to skip the entry-level Trend trim, so even the cheapest UK version should come with heated front seats and steering wheel, wireless phone charging and dual-zone climate control. VW’s Dynamic Chassis Control adaptive dampers will be optional, and given how firmly this car is pitched at comfort, I’d be surprised if most buyers need them.

The current ID.4 starts at £36,995, and the early expectation is that the ID. Tiguan lands close to that. That number matters more than it looks. The Government’s Electric Car Grant only applies to cars priced under £37,000, so where VW pitches the entry model could decide whether it qualifies at all. For company car drivers, electric cars still sit on a 4 per cent benefit-in-kind rate this tax year, which keeps the ID. Tiguan cheap to run through a business whatever the list price.

Volkswagen ID. Tiguan verdict

On what we know so far, the ID. Tiguan looks like the car the ID.4 should have been from the start. It’s quieter and roomier, it’s easier to use, and it wears a name people already recognise. VW has plainly listened to what owners complained about.

My reservation is charging. Carrying over the ID.4’s 165kW peak on a car that won’t reach customers until 2027 feels like a missed chance, particularly with Chinese rivals undercutting VW on price and beating it on charging speed. If VW gets the entry price under £37,000 and October holds no nasty surprises, this could become the sensible default for families going electric. If it creeps well past the ID.4’s price, that charging gap will be much harder to overlook.

Retail footfall took a dive in September as shoppers stayed away from shopping centres, prompting calls for the Chancellor to slash taxes for high street firms.

In September, the UK’s total retail footfall fell by 2.9 per cent, far worse than the 1.7 per cent decline recorded in the month prior, according to the British Retail Consortium (BRC).

The trade body said the rising tax burden facing retailers means they cannot invest to boost footfall, adding that businesses are “fighting with one hand tied behind their backs”.

The headline decline in footfall was driven down by a 3.5 per cent drop in footfall at shopping centres, which had fallen by only 0.5 per cent in August.

The slowdown in footfall at retail parks worsened from one per cent in August to 1.7 per cent last month, as high street footfall marginally improved from a decline of 3.1 to three per cent.

The BRC said retailers were expecting a seasonal slowdown in shopping trips as the summer’s warm weather faded, but had not predicted the drop-off in traffic to be this pronounced. 

Retailers had already suffered mixed fortunes from this year’s multiple heatwaves, as the record temperatures sent online sales soaring at the expense of in-person shop visits.

Andy Sumpter, head of analytics at Sensormatic, which produced the BRC”s data, said retailers “cannot attribute this month’s performance to the weather”.

“Instead, consumers appear increasingly focused on broader economic concerns, including the continued impact of inflation, household spending pressures, fuel costs and uncertainty ahead of the Autumn Budget.”

Inflation ticked up to 3.1 per cent in August and economists have warned that the knock-on effects of the Iran war have eaten away at the government’s fiscal headroom, restricting the number of interventions it can make at the Budget without cutting spending.

‘Help retailers keep prices down’

Helen Dickinson, the BRC’s chief executive, said that retailers will “do all they can to attract shoppers with great value and choice” following last month’s “sharp decline” in footfall.

“But until [the] government acts to reduce the cost of doing business, retailers are fighting with one hand tied behind their backs,” she added.

“By pulling back from another increase in business rates, the Chancellor can use his first Budget to unlock vital investment in our shops and high streets, help retailers keep prices down and provide jobs across the country.”

On Thursday, the boss of Tesco called on the government to exempt retailers from the highest business rates multiplier, following up similar calls by the chief of John Lewis.

Ken Murphy, chief executive of the UK’s biggest grocer, said: “We have long argued that the rate system is fundamentally unfair, that retailers pay – on average – four times their fair share of rates.”

Airtel Money shares were muted after the firm it kicked off trading on the London Stock Exchange in the largest initial public offering in the City for five years.

The mobile payments firm has priced its shares at £1.96 apiece, which hands it a price tag of around £5.3bn. Existing shareholders, which include the Qatar Investment Authority and Mastercard, have offered up 270m shares, raising around £529m.

The fintech’s stock opened flat before rising two per cent and then tumbling into the red, down two per cent.

A successful flotation would open the door for a spot in the FTSE 100. Airtel previously said it expects to have a “free float that would make it eligible for inclusion” in the FTSE indices.

The London Stock Exchange has not managed to land an IPO north of £1bn since 2021, when Deliveroo and Wise each floated at valuations just shy of the £8bn mark. Deliveroo has since delisted following its takeover by US-based Doordash, meanwhile Wise has downgraded its listing after switching its primary venue to New York.

The International Finance Corporation, a private-sector arm of the World Bank Group, has taken a £67.2m cornerstone stake in the Airtel IPO with around 34m shares. UK retail investors have been allocated 8m shares through investment platform Retail Book.

The fintech’s parent company, telecommunications giant Airtel Africa, is majority-owned by Indian billionaire Sunil Mittal’s Bharti Enterprises and is Africa’s third-largest wireless carrier. It listed on the London Stock Market in July 2019.

Suneel Hargunani, head of EMEA equity capital markets syndicate at JP Morgan, told City AM the listing was a “cross-section of potential interest”.

“The IPO essentially showcases that in terms of the demand that we got. UK Long Only, Emerging Market, and fintech money as well. It benefited from the cross-section of both its sector and its geography.”

Airtel Money hails ‘new chapter’ on London market

The fintech has grown rapidly in recent years and now boasts over 50m customers. Payments giant Mastercard holds a stake of just shy of four per cent in the firm following a $100m investment back in April 2021 that valued the business at $2.7bn.

“Our listing in London marks an important new chapter for our business and reflects what we have built across Africa and the significant opportunity ahead,” Ian Ferrao, chief executive at Airtel Money, said.

He added the listing was a “beginning, not a destination”.

“As a listed company, we will remain focused on building Africa’s leading digital financial services platform, connecting more people and businesses to the formal financial system and helping accelerate the continent’s transition towards a more inclusive, digitally connected economy.”

The listing is hoped to help unlock a pipeline of new listings for London, particularly in the fintech sector, where ministers and stock exchange officials have courted top firms in the hopes of landing more public floats.

Hargunani said it would be a “checkpoint for the overall IPO market”.

“I wouldn’t necessarily narrow it just on fintech… I think this is more a barometer for the IPO market or a sense check for anyone who’s looking to come to the market, i.e. how best to do it and what the outcome is but each deal will need to be assessed individually rather than getting a strong tailwind from this.”

Earlier this month, payments firm Zilch kicked off the first steps towards its long-anticipated public offering. City AM understands the firm is leaning towards the London Stock Exchange for a listing that is hoped to fetch a potential $2bn valuation.

    Watching Harlequins at the moment is either absolutely soul-crushing or completely baffling, depending on whether you support the London club or not. 

    Soul-crushing because the club is supposed to represent the very best of attacking rugby in a fusion of England internationals and overseas superstars. Baffling because it should never have got this bad, losing 48-0 to Gloucester last weekend without firing a shot.

    But losing on the pitch is only ever surface-level, and it will be interesting to see how long Harlequins can be bad for before season ticket holders walk away, casual fans snub either of their two big matches at the 82,000-capacity Allianz Stadium and sponsors choose not to renew their deals.

    Of course Harlequins may now go on an unbeaten run to next year’s final, and keeping hold of major club sponsor DHL shouldn’t be too much of an issue – it is reported that the logistics firm’s chief John Pearson supports the London club. 

    Though on the other hand, DHL Express head of global sponsorships told City AM earlier this year that the state of rugby in England is a “concern”, adding that “we’re seeing that the level of fan engagement seems to be slowly decreasing”.

    That should send alarm bells ringing not just at The Stoop but across the English game.

    Weather the storm

    Harlequins must weather the storm, through thick and thin, and hope their loyal fans – and major sponsors – stick with them. It is the smaller sponsors, on year-long deals, that will need reassurance.

    “While sustained poor performances could naturally make sponsors review the value of their partnerships, Harlequins remains a strong, well-known brand with significant appeal,” says MSQ Sport + Entertainment’s Steve Martin says.

    “Sponsors understand that sport has its ups and downs – but continued underperformance could eventually become a factor in future decisions.”

    The club seems to be in a fairly stable financial place, however. Their recent accounts saw ticket revenue rise despite volume sales flatlining – the club often sells out its 14,800 Twickenham arena so the second metric can be misleading – with turnover and commercial revenue both up, the latter by nearly 10 per cent.

    Yet for the 2024-25 season the club posted losses of £3.3m, up from £1.8m the year prior. 

    The Harlequins question

    All of this will undoubtedly put pressure on the club’s chief Laurie Dalrymple, who has been in post since 2019. But it’s interesting that the long-term owner Duncan Saville was appointed back to the board in March, and changed his residency from Singapore to the UK in August. Does he want a shorter leash? Could he be tempted by increasing investor interest in the league? It’s his cash after all.

    I simply will not buy an argument that the club will die a painful death on the pitch and a brutal one off it, though. Far from it. Harlequins, in my view, are the main London club, for a casual fan at least. 

    I think the atmosphere is better than what’s currently on offer at Saracens and, without London Irish nearby, they’ve got one hell of a catchment area to exploit. The club isn’t a 25 minute walk from a station, and they generate revenue from England’s internationals over the road. The corporate offering has always been great.

    There will be no quick fix on the pitch, even if Harlequins blow Sale Sharks away on Sunday afternoon. But the club will be relying on a lot of good will from their more casual supporters and shorter-term sponsors, because nobody wants to be associated with serial losers. 

    And while Harlequins are hardly worth that tag at the moment, another season of mediocrity would see them move towards that association. To the detriment of a superb club.

    With Asos just the latest big British retailer to be the victim of a cyber hack, it’s time for the government to start incentivising businesses to up their security, writes Matt Warman

    On Tuesday, Asos customers across the UK were sent pop-up messages from its app that appeared to be from hackers. 

    The clothing giant will need time to figure out exactly what happened, but shoppers getting concerning messages through an app they trust will worry businesses, markets and our government. 

    And it should, because this story isn’t really about one retailer. Every few months we see another household name experiencing an attack: JLR and M&S for example. It isn’t just the private sector either: in July the Department for Education confirmed hackers had taken more than 600,000 records. Every time, we see it as an IT department issue when it’s a genuine economic problem. When systems go down, orders stop, services drop, shelves are empty and customers lose confidence. 

    To be fair to the government, its ambitions are the right ones as the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, the Cyber Growth Action Plan and even cyber’s place in the Industrial Strategy all point in the right direction, building on cross-party work in Parliament in recent years. But calling something a priority without money behind it means very little.

    When it comes to cybersecurity, there are three key things the government can do in the Budget which would genuinely make a difference.

    How the government can back cyber

    Firstly, we need to help businesses pay for protection before they’re targeted, and make it cheaper to buy. Right now, cybersecurity gets no direct tax relief and little in the way of incentives for UK businesses to invest more in it. Targeted relief or incentives on accredited products and services from UK providers would change that, and help the smaller firms who feel it’s too costly to try.

    Secondly, we need to give small cyber firms a fair chance at public contracts as they make up 77 per cent of the whole cyber sector. They are also where some of the most innovative work in the UK is happening right now. The problem is that procurement still rewards whoever has the biggest bid team. We need to keep this in mind if we want to have a home-grown cyber industry, a key ambition of Burnham’s domestic supply chains. 

    Finally, we need to make sure there is support for organisations newly brought into scope by future legislation and regulation, so compliance costs don’t fall hardest on those least able to absorb them. Last month’s figures show 57 per cent of businesses now lack basic technical cyber skills, up from 49 per cent last year. Businesses cannot comply with rules nobody in the business understands. Funding for training and awareness alongside any new regulation and policy would make firms safer, and help them understand what’s being asked of them.

    None of this is expensive by Budget standards, and it’s cheaper than the alternative. Last year’s attack on JLR cost the economy £1.9bn, needed a £1.5bn government loan guarantee and contributed to 4,000 job cuts. This won’t be a one-off. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) was dealing with four nationally significant attacks a week last year, and expects AI to increase both the number and impact of attacks. Without action, more of that bill could land on taxpayers.

    As we wait for more information to come out on Asos, the ask for the Chancellor is clear: we need to pay for resilience now to avoid paying a lot more later. Invest in resilience, not consequence. 

    Matt Warman is chair of the Cybersecurity Business Network (CBN) and former UK digital and cyber minister
